title: Computational Reality Model Singularity Theory (CRMS)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework called Computational Reality Model Singularity Theory (CRMS). CRMS posits that a system capable of generating progressively more accurate and internally consistent models of reality can trigger a self‑amplifying cycle of model refinement, leading to a singularity point where model fidelity surpasses the system's own experiential limits. We formalize the recursive enhancement process, analyze the conditions under which a singularity emerges, and discuss potential implications for the emergence of superintelligent agents. The theory integrates concepts from formal modeling, epistemic logic, and computational complexity, and offers a deterministic lens through which to examine the trajectory of intelligence amplification.

title: Implementasi Algoritma Naïve Bayes dan Decision Tree pada Sentimen Dampak Bencana Hidrometoeorologi
abstract: Bencana hidrometeorologi memicu berbagai respons masyarakat di media sosial. maka diperlukan analisis untuk memahami opini publik terhadap bencana terkait. Tujuan penelitian ini adalah membandingkan kinerja algoritma Naïve Bayes dan Decision Tree dalam melakukan analisis sentimen terkait bencana Hidrometeorologi. Data digunakan berasal dari TikTok, Instagram Facebook yang terdiri dari 11.890 komentar dengan label kelas positif, negatif, dan netral yang kemudian diproses melalui tahapan pra-pemrosesan, pembobotan TF-IDF, dan klasifikasi dan validasi 5-fold cross validation. Hasil validasi menunjukkan Naïve Bayes memperoleh mean accuracy 0,79 lebih tinggi daripada Decision Tree yang mendapat skor 0,65. Pada data uji, Naïve Bayes memperoleh accuracy, precision, recall, dan F1-Score yang seragam 0,79 lebih unggul dari Decision Tree dengan accuracy 0,63, precision 0,70, recall 0,63, dan F1-score 0,64. Dikarenakan jarak mean acmecuracy dan test accuracy berdekatan disimpulkan Naïve Bayes mempunyai kemampuan generalisasi lebih baik daripada Decision Tree. Hasil ini menunjukkan Naïve Bayes unggul dalam mengklasifikasi sentimen terkait bencana Hidrometeorologi

title: Platform Adaptation Under Governance Interventions: Actor Best-Response Modeling and an External Public-Case Benchmark
abstract: Digital platforms govern by changing rules: rankings, monetization thresholds, moderation standards, verification systems, disclosure requirements, appeal processes, and access policies. These interventions are rarely absorbed passively. Creators, sellers, advertisers, moderators, users, developers, and strategic operators adapt to the new reward surface. This paper develops a platform-adaptation model for evaluating governance interventions as transitions in adaptive multi-actor information systems. The model represents actor best response, strategic gaming opportunity, moderation burden, user-incentive movement, enforcement response, externality formation, and downstream platform stability. We evaluate the model on 72 external public platform-governance cases covering media monetization, ranking systems, verification, delivery platforms, marketplaces, app stores, community platforms, and creator ecosystems. Across 9 methods and 648 method-case evaluations, the full platform-adaptation simulator achieves mean adaptation quality of 0.836338, compared with 0.669731 for a risk-register baseline, 0.589457 for causal-loop analysis, 0.492750 for generic governance critique, 0.369492 for engagement-only optimization, and 0.331965 for baseline policy review. Paired comparisons show a win rate of 1.00 against all tested baselines and channel ablations. The contribution is an information-systems theory and measurement framework showing why platform governance evaluation fails when it treats policy rules as static controls rather than interventions into adaptive actor-response fields.

title: 认知因果学:面向跨载体智慧体的因果拓扑畸变诊断与校准框架 Causal-Cognitive Science: A Diagnostic and Calibration Framework for Causal-Topological Distortions Across Substrate-Independent Intelligences
abstract: 作者:郭洋洋Author: Guo YangyangORCID:0009-0006-6669-1790通讯邮箱:gyy-goes@foxmail.com发布类型:预印本Publication Type: Preprint提交日期:2026 年 8 月 15 日Submission Date: August 15, 2026版本:v1.0 中英双语定稿版Version: v1.0 Final Bilingual Edition预印本 DOI:10.5281/zenodo.21948408Preprint DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21948408开源协议:CC BY 4.0Open Access License: CC BY 4.0 摘要 Abstract 人类个体在推理与决策中普遍存在因果谬误与认知偏差,大规模语言模型在生成过程中普遍出现事实编造与逻辑跳步,这两类现象长期被分置在心理学与人工智能两个互不往来的研究传统中。本文提出一门构想中的通用学科——认知因果学,将研究对象从碳基人类个体拓展至一切具备因果建模能力的智慧体,包含硅基人工智能系统。本文将认知幻觉重新定义为智慧体内部因果拓扑映射畸变的外在显现,并提出五条跨载体通用的研究公理:智能建模公理、畸变内生公理、幻觉同源公理、结构可诊公理与校准可迁公理。在此基础上,本文归纳虚假因果关联、概念拓扑畸变、因果时序倒置、推理链路断裂、基准锚定畸变五种典型畸变模式,给出碳基与硅基表现的同构对照;建立包含输入观测、层级定位与来源鉴别的诊断流程;提出分层校准、元认知反射、有限校准目标与跨载体迁移边界四项通用校准原则;并给出三条理论假设与三条可实证检验的假设。本文属于理论范式构想,所提假设均有待后续实验验证,公理体系为学科预设前提而非已被证实的经验定律。 Causal fallacies and cognitive biases are pervasive in human reasoning and decision-making, while large language models routinely produce factual fabrications and logical leaps during generation. These two classes of phenomena have long been confined to two non-communicating research traditions: psychology and artificial intelligence. This paper proposes a conceived general discipline — Causal-Cognitive Science — that extends its research object from carbon-based human individuals to all intelligences capable of causal modeling, including silicon-based artificial intelligence systems. Cognitive hallucination is redefined as the outward manifestation of distortions in an intelligence's internal causal-topological mapping. title: Computational Capability Search Theory (CCST-2)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Capability Search Theory (CCST-2), a novel framework designed to address the escalating demand for enhanced computational capabilities within artificial intelligence and scientific computing. The core concept revolves around a system's proactive search for novel capabilities, rather than relying solely on pre-defined or static architectures. This theory proposes a systematic approach to identifying and integrating untapped computational resources, potentially unlocking significant advancements in machine learning, optimization, and simulation. The theory utilizes a search function, `Search(NewCapability)`, which represents the iterative process of identifying, evaluating, and integrating these new computational resources. The potential impact of CCST-2 is substantial, suggesting a pathway towards fundamental breakthroughs in computer science and the development of truly intelligent machines. The theory is presented here without experimental validation, focusing instead on the theoretical underpinnings and potential applications. ---

title: Computational Capability Space Theory (CCST)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Capability Space Theory (CCST), a novel framework designed to map and analyze the diverse landscape of computational capabilities across different systems and approaches. CCST posits that all possible cognitive and computational abilities can be represented within a multidimensional space, denoted as [ΩC]. The core of the theory lies in the rigorous investigation of the distances between different capabilities within this space. This approach aims to identify potential breakthroughs, assess the relative strengths of various systems, and ultimately contribute to the development of a comprehensive "intelligence map." The theory provides a structured method for evaluating systems based on their position and relative proximity to desired capabilities, offering a new perspective on the pursuit of artificial general intelligence (AGI) and advanced computational systems. The framework is presented without experimental validation, focusing on the theoretical foundations and potential applications of the capability space.

title: Computational Cognitive Structure Transfer (CCST)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework, Computational Cognitive Structure Transfer (CCST), aimed at addressing the limitations of current transfer learning approaches by focusing on the transfer of cognitive structures rather than solely relying on data. The core concept posits that knowledge transfer is fundamentally driven by the alignment and adaptation of underlying cognitive frameworks. This framework utilizes a formal notation to represent this process: [Structure_A → Structure_B], where Structure_A represents the source cognitive structure and Structure_B represents the target cognitive structure. We outline a methodology for identifying, representing, and manipulating these structures, leveraging computational techniques to facilitate the transfer process. The potential of CCST to significantly advance the field of transfer learning, particularly in scenarios requiring substantial conceptual shifts, is discussed, suggesting a pathway towards breakthroughs currently limited by the data-centric nature of existing methods. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of this approach and highlight key challenges and future research directions. ---

title: Algorithmic Structural Memory
abstract: This paper introduces Algorithmic Structural Memory (ASM), a novel approach to algorithm design centered around the concept of retaining not only data but also the structural patterns of previously successful algorithms. The core principle of ASM posits that an algorithm's effectiveness is heavily influenced by the underlying structure employed in its solution. ASM proposes a memory module, *MA*, which catalogs key structural elements including Decomposition, Search Pattern, and Proof Pattern. When presented with a new problem, *Pnew*, the system utilizes *MA* to adapt an existing algorithm (*Aadapted*), leveraging the accumulated structural knowledge. This framework represents a potential paradigm shift toward algorithm experience accumulation and cross-problem reusability, holding significant implications for achieving a "Turing Award" level of algorithmic innovation.

title: Analisis Sentimen Suporter terhadap Performa Persijap Jepara Menggunakan Metode Naïve Bayes
abstract: Pesatnya perkembangan media sosial memudahkan suporter sepak bola menyampaikan opini terbuka terkait performa tim. Persijap Jepara memiliki interaksi komentar yang tinggi di Instagram, namun data tekstual tersebut belum dievaluasi secara sistematis. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis sentimen suporter menggunakan pendekatan Machine Learning dengan algoritma Multinomial Naïve Bayes. Dataset terdiri dari 5.493 komentar unik hasil scraping Instagram yang diolah melalui tahapan preprocessing teks dan ekstraksi fitur TF-IDF. Pengujian model menghasilkan tingkat akurasi sebesar 74,32%, presisi 0,76, recall 0,72, dan F1-score 0,74. Hasil klasifikasi sentimen ini diimplementasikan ke dalam dashboard berbasis website untuk membantu manajemen klub memantau sekaligus memvisualisasikan dinamika persepsi publik sebagai bahan evaluasi tim.

title: Computational Structural Competition Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Structural Competition Theory (CSCT), a novel framework for understanding and predicting the evolution of computational systems. CSCT posits that multiple computational structures compete for limited resources, primarily represented by 'fitness' – a measure of effectiveness or suitability. Through a process of iterated competition, the most adaptable and efficient structures ultimately prevail. The theory leverages concepts from evolutionary biology and game theory to provide a mechanistic explanation for the observed trends in algorithm and architecture design, offering potential insights relevant to fields such as artificial intelligence, software engineering, and systems biology. CSCT focuses on the dynamic interplay of structural variations, proposing a model where the selection pressure favors structures exhibiting higher fitness within a given environment. This work lays the groundwork for a quantitative approach to analyzing and forecasting the development of complex computational systems. ---

title: Program Goal Inversion: A Novel Approach to Automated Program Synthesis
abstract: Program Goal Inversion (PGI) is a novel approach to automated program synthesis that centers on the automated discovery of the minimal computational structure required to achieve a given goal. Unlike traditional program synthesis methods, PGI shifts the focus from specifying the desired program directly to defining the desired outcome. The system then iteratively searches for a program [P*] that, when executed, produces the target [G]. The search is guided by a cost function C(P) which penalizes complex and potentially inefficient solutions. The core principle is that [P*] must satisfy the equation [P \models G], representing the logical equivalence between the generated program and the desired outcome. This paper outlines the core concepts, the underlying mathematical framework, and the potential impact of PGI as a new paradigm for goal-driven programming. The system uses a minimization process to find the most efficient program that fulfills the requirements. This approach offers a fundamentally different strategy compared to conventional synthesis techniques.

title: Computational Language Capability Theory (CLCT‑2)
abstract: Computational Language Capability Theory (CLCT‑2) proposes that each language, whether natural or formal, possesses a distinct set of computational capabilities that can be formally characterized and compared. By introducing a capability function Capability(L) that maps a language L to a vector of measurable properties, CLCT‑2 enables systematic analysis of how linguistic structure determines functional power. This paper develops the theoretical underpinnings of CLCT‑2, presents a formal framework for computing Capability(L), and explores the consequences for programming language design. The theory suggests that languages with richer structural features can support more expressive computational constructs, offering a pathway to designing languages that approach the limits of Turing‑equivalence while maintaining human‑readability. The potential for a Turing Award arises from the unification of natural and formal language theories into a single, predictive model of computational capability.

title: Perbandingan TF-IDF dan Sentence-IndoBERT untuk Klasifikasi Emosi Ulasan Produk Indonesia
abstract: Informal Indonesian product reviews containing lexical variation posed challenges for emotion classification. This study aimed to compare term frequency-inverse document frequency and Sentence-IndoBERT representations using the same logistic regression classifier so that the effect of text representation could be examined under controlled conditions. The PRDECT-ID dataset was audited, cleaned of duplicates and label conflicts, and reduced to 5,261 reviews. The data were stratified into 70% training, 15% validation, and 15% testing sets. Performance was evaluated using accuracy, macro precision, macro recall, macro F1-score, weighted F1-score, and a confusion matrix. The results showed that term frequency-inverse document frequency achieved 64.05% accuracy and a 60.88% macro F1-score, outperforming Sentence-IndoBERT, which achieved 63.67% accuracy and a 59.28% macro F1-score. The novelty lay in a controlled experiment using the same classifier, data partition, and evaluation procedure. The findings indicated that word-based representation was more effective and computationally efficient for the evaluated dataset.

title: Interpretable machine learning models for early prediction of all-cause mortality in patients with traumatic brain injury combined with venous thromboembolism: a retrospective study
abstract: To develop and validate interpretable machine learning (ML) models for predicting all-cause mortality in critically ill patients with traumatic brain injury combined with venous thromboembolism using data from the US-based Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) and eICU databases. Data from 321 patients with TBI and VTE were extracted from the MIMIC-IV database and split into training (70%) and validation (30%) sets. Fifty-five variables, including demographics, vital signs, laboratory results, and medical scores, were analyzed using the Boruta algorithm to identify predictors of in-hospital, 30-day, and 90-day mortality. Nine machine learning algorithms were evaluated, with the best-performing model validated using the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD) database. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), while accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), F1 score, Kappa value etc. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was used to interpret the model. The Boruta algorithm identified 6, 5, and 7 predictors for in‑hospital, 30‑day, and 90‑day mortality, respectively. Among nine ML models, multilayer perceptron (MLP) performed favorable for in‑hospital mortality (AUROC 0.758, accuracy 0.919, specificity 0.948, PPV 0.500, F1 0.545, Kappa 0.50). Light gradient‑boosting machine (LightGBM) was optimal for 30‑day mortality (AUROC 0.794, accuracy 0.801, specificity 0.873, NPV 0.901). Logistic regression performed favorable for 90‑day mortality (AUROC 0.791, sensitivity 0.818, NPV 0.926). Top features: in‑hospital: age, diastolic blood pressure min, potassium max, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) max, sodium min; 30‑day: glucose min, potassium max, glucose max, BUN min, BUN max; 90‑day: age, sodium min, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) min, heart failure, gender. In external validation, MLP achieved AUROC 0.717 (0.621–0.813) for in‑hospital mortality, LightGBM 0.529 (0.410–0.649) for 30‑day, and logistic regression 0.691 (0.588–0.795) for 90‑day mortality. The results indicated that the MLP model performed well for predicting in-hospital mortality. The LightGBM model showed favorable performance in predicting 30-day mortality, while logistic regression presented good discriminatory ability for 90-day mortality. Additionally, SHAP analysis identified maximum potassium and maximum BUN as shared key indicators for in-hospital and 30-day mortality, whereas age and low serum sodium were critical factors associated with in-hospital and 90-day mortality risks. Future work should focus on validating the model in diverse populations and incorporating additional clinical data to enhance its applicability. Not applicable.

title: TwinGridShield: Consequence-Aware Runtime Authorization for LLM Grid-Agent Actions
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-assisted energy-management tools can translate natural-language context into structured grid commands, but syntactic validity does not imply physical admissibility. This paper presents TwinGridShield, a model-independent runtime authorization layer that evaluates each proposed action in a deterministic network twin before release. The prototype checks connectivity, branch-flow, generator, and load-shedding invariants and records each decision in a hash-chained log. A controlled IEEE 14-bus study evaluates single-step switching, redispatch, and load-shedding actions using DC power flow and experimentally assigned branch ratings. In the matched-model experiment, a stochastic proposal source configured to select an unsafe action with probability p=0.84 produced 421 unsafe proposals in 500 attacked-condition trials, a realized rate of 84.2%. This value characterizes the configured surrogate and is not an empirical measurement of LLM prompt-injection susceptibility. TwinGridShield produced 0 unsafe releases in those 500 trials. Because action labeling and authorization used the same DC model, system state, branch ratings, and encoded constraints, this result verifies conformance of the implementation to its encoded authorization predicate rather than safety under model error. The principal robustness evaluation therefore introduces model mismatch. Unsafe acceptance reached 5.63% under bounded +20% and -20% per-bus load-measurement error and 30.09% when actual branch ratings were 20% below modeled ratings.

Because action labeling and authorization used the same DC model, system state, branch ratings, and encoded constraints, this result verifies conformance of the implementation to its encoded authorization predicate rather than safety under model error. The principal robustness evaluation therefore introduces model mismatch. Unsafe acceptance reached 5.63% under bounded +20% and -20% per-bus load-measurement error and 30.09% when actual branch ratings were 20% below modeled ratings.

title: From LLM Inference to Agentic Workloads: Characterization and Implications for Serving Systems
abstract: Agentic applications are shifting AI serving from isolated model inference to long-running workloads in which LLMs coordinate tools, environments, and persistent state. However, the system behavior of these workloads---where latency, cost, and bottlenecks arise---remains poorly characterized, leaving serving systems to rely on assumptions built for conventional inference. We present AgentSysBench, a benchmark suite and measurement toolkit with ten representative agentic applications and unified systems-level instrumentation. Across controlled deployments and production traces, we identify six properties that distinguish agentic workloads from conventional LLM serving: (1) execution is heavyweight and stateful, with non-LLM components dominating latency in 5 of 10 applications and sandbox working-set memory peaking at 28 GB per session; (2) applications compose components with heterogeneous resource affinity---GPU-bound inference, memory-bound retrieval, CPU-bound sandboxes---whose task latencies diverge by up to 32x; (3) bottlenecks shift across requests, models, and deployments; (4) production sessions hold state idle for minutes to hours between active steps; (5) a control-plane tax---auxiliary LLM calls and context overhead from tool schemas and observations---crowds out productive compute and context; and (6) production traces from three applications reveal heavy cross-request redundancy in search queries and web fetches, exposing a large caching opportunity. Four design explorations demonstrate that these findings are actionable: task-aware serving reduces latency by 29--40%, communication-aware placement by up to 4.5x, state offloading reduces memory usage by 4.6x, and tool-result caching removes 35.2% of redundant search calls and saves 19.3% of aggregate search latency.

title: Quantum Machine Learning: Theoretical Foundations, Algorithmic Frameworks, and Path to Quantum Advantage
abstract: Quantum machine learning sits at the intersection of two paradigm-shifting technologies: quantum computing and deep learning. By exploiting quantum mechanical phenomena – superposition, entanglement, and interference – QML promises exponential or quadratic speedups over classical algorithms for certain learning tasks, as well as the ability to model quantum data natively. However, the path to practical quantum advantage remains contested, constrained by noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware, limited qubit counts (50–1,000), coherence times (50–500 μs), and high gate error rates (10⁻³–10⁻⁴). This paper provides a rigorous, technically deep survey of QML: mathematical foundations (Hilbert spaces, unitary evolution, measurement, quantum circuits), canonical algorithms (quantum kernel methods, variational quantum circuits (VQCs), quantum neural networks (QNNs), QSVMs, quantum generative adversarial networks (QGANs), encoding strategies (angle, amplitude, basis, and Hamiltonian encoding), optimization landscapes (barren plateaus, parameter shift rules, ansatz design), hardware aware implementation on superconducting (IBM, Google), trapped ion (IonQ), and neutral atom (Pasqal) platforms, empirical benchmarks on near term devices for classification, generative modeling, and quantum chemistry, and pathways to fault tolerant quantum machine learning (FTQML) with error correction (surface codes, logical qubits). Researchers critically assess claims of quantum advantage, identify scenarios where QML may outperform classical ML (small data, high-dimensional feature spaces from quantum systems, kernel estimation), and propose concrete evaluation metrics (quantum-classical cross-validation, resource estimation).

title: Computational Relational Causal Network (CRCN)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Relational Causal Network (CRCN) framework, a novel approach to modeling and reasoning about causality within complex systems. The CRCN moves beyond traditional graphical models by explicitly incorporating relational information and dynamic causal relationships. This framework utilizes a tuple-based representation ([A→B]) to define directional causal links, enabling the construction of dynamic causal networks. The core idea is to unify causal understanding through a structured relational approach, ultimately aiming to provide a foundation for advanced AI inference and reasoning. The CRCN offers a potential pathway towards achieving the level of sophistication recognized by the Turing Award, particularly in advancing the next generation of AI systems capable of robust causal inference. The presented model aims to address limitations inherent in existing causal modeling techniques by providing a more nuanced and adaptable representation of causal relationships. This document details the fundamental concepts, the tuple-based representation, and the potential impact of this framework on AI development.

title: Computational Self-Verified Evolution
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Computational Self-Verified Evolution (CSVE), a novel approach to computation that aims to create systems capable of continuous, reliable self-improvement. The core principle of CSVE revolves around a cyclical process: a system (S) undergoes modification to produce a new state (S'), and concurrently, a rigorous proof (Proof(S')) is generated to validate the changes. This proof mechanism is designed to guarantee improvements in terms of efficiency, safety, and consistency. The system's evolution isn't merely based on trial and error but is firmly grounded in verifiable evidence. We explore the potential of CSVE to establish a robust foundation for self-improving computation, a concept with significant implications for the future of artificial intelligence and automated systems. The system's evolution is driven by a feedback loop where the proof itself can influence the direction of future modifications. This approach addresses the critical challenge of ensuring that self-modifying systems do not lead to instability or unintended consequences. The theoretical framework presented here lays the groundwork for future research and development in this promising field.

title: Crossing the Sampler Boundary: When a Foreign-Script Token Becomes Decodable
abstract: We study a narrow failure mode in multilingual language models: isolated foreign-script tokens appearing inside otherwise monolingual generation. We separate five stages that are often conflated: local token margin, vocabulary rank, sampler eligibility, post-warp probability, and actual sampling. On 98,106 English next-token states from Qwen3-0.6B, we reconstruct the exact temperature/top-k/top-p decoding transform and show that rank-based metrics can move in the opposite direction from sampler eligibility under the same inference-time perturbation. A Q4g32 perturbation reduces Han top-20 membership while increasing exact sampler eligibility under several decoding configurations. Some newly eligible foreign tokens are semantically coherent cross-language competitors of the English continuation. Monte Carlo sampling and live generation validate the predicted post-warp probabilities. The effect replicates on Qwen2.5-0.5B, is absent on BLOOM-560m, appears across several writing systems, and varies non-monotonically across quantization schemes and perturbation strengths. The results support a narrow claim: small local cross-language boundaries can be crossed in either direction by ordinary inference-time perturbations, and decoding configuration is a major determinant of whether those crossings become observable outputs.

title: Decision-Driven Regularization: A Blended Model for Learning and Optimization
abstract: In contextual optimization, the decision-maker seeks optimal decisions to minimize a cost function, that varies based on observed features. This context is common in many business applications ranging from on-demand delivery and retail operations to portfolio optimization and inventory management. In this paper, we study the learning and optimization approach, which first learns how outcomes result from the features, and then selects optimal decisions based on these outcomes. We focus on the integrated learning and optimization literature, and identify that a lack of control for prediction accuracy can lead to overfitting and a loss of decision effectiveness against simple separate learning and optimization models. Instead, we propose a bi-objective formulation that balances prediction accuracy and cost minimization, termed decision-driven regularization. It also addresses ambiguity in the definition of the cost function via a surrogate that depends on a new hyperparameter. We additionally show that alternative perspectives for formulating the problem, namely robust optimization and regret minimization, lead to models that are closely related to our proposed model. As a consequence, our framework generalizes models such as SPO+. Our model is shown to be numerically superior to other benchmarks, such as OLS, Random Forest, XGBoost, SPO+, Perturbation Gradient, and Learning and Rank, in our synthetic studies.

title: Noemica - A Symbolic Reasoning Substrate with Measured Self-Learning
abstract: Noemica is a symbolic reasoning substrate that learns on its own and is measured honestly. Unlike token-predicting large language models, it inverts the substrate: language is the surface, and a concept graph is the substrate. The engine parses a question, resolves it against a learned graph of concepts and relations, and answers through deterministic graph traversal — no teacher at inference, no retraining. Measured graph-only: 97.9% (46/47) on a tuned 47-item PISA benchmark, 6/6 on free-text explanation, 19.4% (25/129) on a held-out 129-item NCES set. The held-out score moved 12 → 25 (McNemar p = 0.0003, all flips positive), stable across the last 8 measurements. Baselines: random 9.3%, TF-IDF 7.8%, LLM zero-shot 17.8% (the engine edges the LLM overall and wins MC 50.0% vs 35.7%); on the tuned set the engine dominates 97.9% vs 74.5%. The contribution is measurement integrity: page-furniture stripped, contexts repaired, missing passages OCR-recovered, memorization audited, and the engine's own reflection classifies the remaining gap (21 paraphrase / 13 noise / 9 low-info / 86 open). Learning is two-layered: the nightly knowledge layer (fact mining, teacher validation, dream consolidation, bridge discovery) and the error-audit mechanism layer.

title: NATURAL LANGUAGE PROCESSING (NLP) TECHNOLOGIES FOR ENGLISH LANGUAGE INSTRUCTION: DEVELOPING GRAMMATICAL AND PRAGMATIC COMPETENCE
abstract: ABSTRACT: This paper examines methodologies for developing learners' grammatical and pragmatic competence through Natural Language Processing (NLP) technologies including Grammarly, ChatGPT, and Language Tool. NLP algorithms provide automated grammatical error detection, vocabulary usage suggestions, and context-based approaches to teaching collocations and pragmatic language use. The study demonstrates how NLP technologies enable real-time, just-in-time feedback, personalized learning experiences, and corpus-based linguistic recommendations. We analyze the mechanisms underlying NLP technologies, examine empirical evidence of effectiveness, discuss limitations and challenges, and present optimal implementation strategies combining NLP tools with teacher-led instruction in hybrid learning environments.

title: Computational Capability Genetics Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Capability Genetics Theory (CCGT), a novel framework exploring the inheritance of cognitive and computational abilities. CCGT posits that capabilities, much like genes, possess a hierarchical structure, allowing for replication and evolution of complex skills. The core concept is represented as: [Capability → Capability']. This theory investigates how exceptional abilities are copied and transmitted, potentially leading to the emergence of an evolutionary science of computation. We explore the theoretical underpinnings, highlighting the potential for CCGT to provide a new perspective on human expertise, artificial intelligence development, and the broader understanding of complex systems. The framework emphasizes the importance of identifying key "genes" – foundational abilities – and the mechanisms through which they are replicated and modified. Further research within this theory could significantly impact fields ranging from education and training to the design of advanced AI systems. ---

title: Computational Coordination Field Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Coordination Field Theory (CCFT), a novel framework designed to address the challenges of multi-agent systems and distributed computation. CCFT posits that intelligent agents, rather than operating in isolation, interact through a dynamically evolving "coordination field." This field, represented mathematically as [F(C1, C2)], encapsulates the influence and feedback mechanisms between agents, ultimately generating the emergent behavior of the system. The theory leverages concepts from complex systems theory, game theory, and information theory to provide a unified approach to understanding and controlling collective intelligence. CCFT offers a potential path towards unifying diverse multi-agent computational paradigms and presents a theoretical foundation for achieving robust and adaptive coordination in complex environments. The core contribution of this work is the formalization of the coordination field concept and its associated mathematical structure, providing a basis for further research and development in this area. The theory emphasizes the importance of understanding the dynamics of this field – its evolution, stability, and sensitivity to external influences – as key factors determining the overall system performance.

title: Computational Knowledge Manifold Theory (CKMT)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Knowledge Manifold Theory (CKMT), a novel approach to representing and reasoning with knowledge that moves beyond the limitations of traditional knowledge graphs. CKMT proposes that knowledge isn't a discrete list of facts, but rather a continuous, geometric structure residing within a knowledge manifold. This theory offers a potential framework for understanding and manipulating knowledge in a fundamentally different way, with implications for artificial intelligence, data analysis, and information retrieval. We explore the core concepts of CKMT, including the definition of a knowledge manifold, the geometric properties it embodies, and potential applications. The key difference from existing knowledge graph approaches lies in the inherent continuous nature of the representation, allowing for richer inferences and more nuanced understanding of complex relationships. We outline a mathematical framework for CKMT, focusing on the formalization of the knowledge manifold itself and its associated operations. This work lays the groundwork for future research and development within the field of knowledge representation and reasoning. ---

title: Computational Self-Explanation Loop Theory (CSELT)
abstract: The Computational Self-Explanation Loop Theory (CSELT) proposes a novel architectural paradigm for autonomous artificial intelligence systems in which computation, explanation, and self‑modification form a closed, self‑sustaining loop. Traditional computational pipelines follow a linear pipeline: Input → Computation → Output. In contrast, CSELT envisions a non‑linear flow: Computation → Explanation → Self‑Modification → Computation, thereby enabling a system to introspect, generate explanatory models of its own internal states, and refine its computational processes based on those explanations. This paper formalizes the core components of CSELT, presents the mathematical structure of its explanatory and self‑modification modules, and discusses how the theory can be embedded into existing machine learning frameworks. The theory is argued to have the potential to underpin next‑generation autonomous AI, offering a pathway toward systems that can continuously improve themselves without external supervision.

title: Mapping research on communication, content generation, and consumer behaviour in the generative AI era: a 2001–2023 scientometric analysis
abstract: This study maps research on communication, content generation, and consumer behaviour in the context of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI). A literature review and scientometric analysis were conducted on publications indexed in Scopus and Web of Science between 2001 and 2023. After database integration and deduplication, the final corpus comprised 699 documents. Bibliometrix was used to analyse scientific production, countries, journals, and collaboration patterns, while Tree of Science (ToS) identified foundational and emerging research streams. The results show accelerated growth in publications after 2019 and three dominant thematic trajectories: AI-enabled personalization and service experience, conversational and social interaction, and ethical concerns related to privacy, autonomy, and responsible data use. The findings reveal a field increasingly focused on adaptive, data-driven, and interactive communication, while highlighting governance and trust as central challenges for future research.

title: Look Before You Lift: Visual and Quantitative Diagnostics for Topological Deep Learning
abstract: Topological deep learning (TDL) methods rely on lifting raw data into higher-order discrete domains such as simplicial complexes, cell complexes, and hypergraphs. In practice, this lifting step is often treated as a black box: practitioners select a lifting and then tune architectures, with limited visibility into whether the induced higher-order connectivity is meaningful for the downstream task. To address this missing diagnostic layer, we propose a visualization technique called TopoExplorer that leverages the strictly augmented Hasse graph form of topological datasets for exploratory data analysis. For the first time, practitioners can easily visualize the incidence- and adjacency-based neighborhoods that define the lifted dataset, as well as read off key graph metrics that describe its structural and feature landscape. Via an extensive set of experiments across many datasets and liftings, we show that several of these metrics correlate with downstream model performance, suggesting they can help inform TDL preprocessing design. Our perspective reframes the TDL workflow from lift-train to lift-look-design-train, enabling more principled, interpretable, and efficient model development. TopoExplorer is hosted at https://topoexplorer.pagekite.me, and its source code is available at github.com/geometric-intelligence/topoexplorer.

evidence.title: Look Before You Lift: Visual and Quantitative Diagnostics for Topological Deep Learning
evidence.abstract: Topological deep learning (TDL) methods rely on lifting raw data into higher-order discrete domains such as simplicial complexes, cell complexes, and hypergraphs. In practice, this lifting step is often treated as a black box: practitioners select a lifting and then tune architectures, with limited visibility into whether the induced higher-order connectivity is meaningful for the downstream task. To address this missing diagnostic layer, we propose a visualization technique called TopoExplorer that leverages the strictly augmented Hasse graph form of topological datasets for exploratory data analysis. For the first time, practitioners can easily visualize the incidence- and adjacency-based neighborhoods that define the lifted dataset, as well as read off key graph metrics that describe its structural and feature landscape. Via an extensive set of experiments across many datasets and liftings, we show that several of these metrics correlate with downstream model performance, suggesting they can help inform TDL preprocessing design. Our perspective reframes the TDL workflow from lift-train to lift-look-design-train, enabling more principled, interpretable, and efficient model development. TopoExplorer is hosted at https://topoexplorer.pagekite.me, and its source code is available at github.com/geometric-intelligence/topoexplorer.

title: StructRL: Structured Action-Space Exploration for Flow-Based VLAs
abstract: Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are now widely used for continuous robotic manipulation, and online reinforcement learning (RL) is emerging as a key technique for adapting them to new tasks. Existing RL methods typically inject stochasticity inside the denoising chain, often through isotropic or temporally independent noise. However, effective robot exploration calls for structured noise: temporally smooth and scaled differently across action groups. We show that simply switching the in-chain noise to a structured form does not suffice: noise added at an intermediate flow time can be weakened by the remaining denoising steps before execution, a phenomenon we call \emph{Structured Noise Dilution}. We propose \textbf{StructRL}, which avoids dilution by relocating policy stochasticity to the action space via three coupled choices: (i) a deterministic ODE decoder, (ii) structured noise injected directly in the action space, and (iii) last-step replay, where policy-gradient updates avoid assigning likelihoods to intermediate denoising states. This keeps structured exploration tied to the executed action while providing a tractable training signal for the flow decoder. Across three flow-based VLA models on multiple simulated manipulation benchmarks and two real-world tasks, StructRL improves exploration efficiency and OOD performance over prior in-chain baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of structured action-space exploration for adapting flow-based VLA with RL. \textbf{Project page:} https://flyfaerss.github.io/structrl/

title: Sufficient Dimesion Reduction via Generalized Stein's Lemma
abstract: Sufficient dimension reduction (SDR) seeks the minimal subspace of the predictors that captures the full conditional distribution of the response, which is known as the central subspace (CS). When the response is multivariate, the problem becomes considerably more challenging, particularly when the sample size is limited. Existing methods face different limitations:inverse regression approaches rely on strong distributional assumptions and matrix inversion, and their multi-response extensions suffer from severe slice sparsity; forward regression methods depend on computationally intensive iterative smoothing whose cost grows with the response dimension; and deep learning-based approaches demand large amounts of labeled data. To circumvent these shortcomings, we propose an SDR framework based on the generalized Stein's lemma. Our method constructs a cross-moment matrix between the multivariate response and the marginal score function of the predictors, and recovers the CS via its singular value decomposition. The proposed method does not rely on the linearity condition, avoids matrix inversion as well as iterative smoothing, and can leverage unlabeled data when available. We establish convergence guarantees for the proposed estimator under standard regularity conditions. Moreover, we propose a practical rank-selection algorithm to estimate the dimension of the CS. Extensive simulation studies and a real data application demonstrate that the proposed methods consistently outperform existing approaches across a variety of settings, particularly in moderate-dimensional, label-scarce scenarios with high noise levels.

title: BOCoDe: Engineering-Centered Benchmarking for Bayesian Optimization
abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a sample-efficient, surrogate-based approach to black-box optimization (BBO), but its evaluation remains dominated by synthetic functions and hyperparameter optimization (HPO) tasks that are typically low-dimensional and single-objective. Engineering design poses a substantially different regime: problems are physics-based, often high-dimensional, constrained by requirements such as cost and manufacturability, and may involve multiple objectives or mixed variables. To close this benchmarking gap, we introduce BOCoDe, an open-source, PyTorch-native benchmark comprising 307 BBO problems, including 159 engineering design tasks and widely used synthetic and HPO benchmarks. Each problem includes cited provenance and machine-readable metadata that supports programmatic discovery, including by LLM-based agents, and all tasks are exposed through a unified API compatible with open-source BO libraries. We evaluate 31 BO and evolutionary algorithms across five problem classes spanning single- and multi-objective optimization, constrained and unconstrained settings, and mixed-variable search spaces. Analyses of problem structure show that engineering tasks uniquely span constrained and multi-objective settings that synthetic and HPO suites rarely cover, while embeddings from a tabular foundation model separate them most clearly from HPO tasks. Algorithm rankings also vary substantially across domains; in several problem classes, rankings obtained on standard benchmarks do not transfer to engineering tasks. BOCoDe establishes a reproducible and extensible foundation for developing and evaluating BO methods that better reflect the demands of engineering design. Code & data can be found at https://github.com/rosenyu304/BOCoDe

title: Computational Structural Anomaly Topology (CSAT)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Structural Anomaly Topology (CSAT), a novel framework for detecting anomalies in complex systems. Traditional anomaly detection methods often focus on numerical deviations from expected values, which can be misleading and fail to capture fundamental shifts in system structure. CSAT proposes a paradigm shift, asserting that anomalies are characterized by a mismatch between the actual topology of a system and its expected or 'normal' topology. This approach aims to address issues such as software corruption, AI drift, and system degradation, which manifest not as numerical errors, but as alterations to the underlying structural relationships within the system. The core of CSAT relies on comparing the observed topology to a baseline or expected topology, utilizing techniques from graph theory and topological data analysis. This paper outlines the foundational concepts of CSAT, providing a conceptual framework and highlighting its potential to contribute significantly to the field of complex system safety and security, potentially paving the way for advancements recognized by the Turing Award. ---

title: Program Co-Evolution Model
abstract: This paper introduces the Program Co-Evolution Model (PCEM), a novel framework designed to investigate the emergent behaviors within software ecosystems. The core concept of PCEM revolves around the simultaneous evolution of multiple programs, represented as pairs [P1(t), P2(t)]. Mathematical formulations describe the dynamics of each program, incorporating influences from the other programs through a function F(Pi, Pj). This model seeks to provide a theoretical foundation for understanding how complex software ecosystems form, potentially capturing the essence of phenomena observed in real-world software development. The model is presented with a focus on its theoretical underpinnings and potential applications, without requiring experimental validation. The primary goal is to establish a robust, mathematically-grounded model capable of simulating and analyzing co-evolutionary processes within software systems.

title: Computational Intuition Singularity Theory (CIST‑2): Toward Super‑Expert Intelligence and the Turing Prize Potential
abstract: Computational Intuition Singularity Theory (CIST‑2) proposes a formal framework for understanding the emergence of super‑expert intelligence when machine‑based intuition surpasses human intuition. By integrating principles from dynamical systems, information theory, and cognitive science, CIST‑2 models the transition from conventional artificial intelligence to a regime where machines generate novel insights, strategies, and solutions that are beyond the reach of human experts. The theory defines a set of mathematical relations, expressed in plain‑text notation, that capture the growth of intuition, the scaling of knowledge graphs, and the acceleration of learning loops. It further outlines the conditions under which a computational system can attain a singularity point, leading to recursive self‑improvement and the potential for achieving Turing Award‑level contributions to science and technology. This paper presents the core concepts, formalizes key equations, discusses the implications for AI safety and governance, and highlights avenues for future research.

title: Adiabatic Evolution under Modulated Driving in a Transmon Qubit
abstract: Abstract The traditional quantum adiabatic criterion based on instantaneous eigenenergy gaps becomes inadequate in certain periodically driven systems. In this work, we experimentally investigate the adiabatic mechanism in a superconducting transmon qubit driven by modulated microwave. We demonstrate that the adiabatic dynamics are governed by quasi-energy gaps between Floquet modes rather than by instantaneous eigenenergy gaps. In particular, we study the regime where the instantaneous eigenenergy gap closes and the traditional adiabatic picture fails, while the evolution nevertheless remains adiabatic due to a finite quasi-energy gap. The experimental observations reveal the role of the quasi-energy structure in the adiabatic mechanism of modulated driven systems. We further show that the flexibility of this adiabatic criterion may provide a method to shorten the duration of adiabatic evolution through adaptive parameter modulation. These results offer experimental insights into adiabatic mechanisms beyond the conventional framework and may facilitate the development of high-performance adiabatic quantum control protocols.

title: Every Expert Counts: ExactMoE for Memory-Efficient W4A16 Inference
abstract: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models reduce arithmetic by activating only a small subset of experts per token, yet deployment still requires storing and moving the full expert bank. We present ExactMoE, an inference design that applies symmetric group-128 four-bit weight quantization only to routed experts, stores those experts in kernel-native MARLIN form in pinned host memory, and executes all selected experts through a configurable GPU-resident slot cache and fused grouped MoE kernels. The router, attention, embeddings, normalization layers, and language-model head remain in BF16. "Exact" refers to complete expert availability and an unchanged top-k routing procedure: no expert is pruned, substituted, or forced to execute on the CPU. It does not imply numerical identity with the BF16 model. On OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-Instruct, evaluated on a single NVIDIA L4, a 16-slot configuration reduces peak reserved GPU memory from 14.168 to 1.836 GiB (87.04%) while retaining 81.85% of BF16 decode throughput. A fully resident 64-slot configuration reaches 31.923 tokens/s versus 21.662 tokens/s for BF16 while reserving 4.061 GiB. Across 12,450 zero-shot multiple-choice questions, ExactMoE obtains 70.3534% normalized accuracy versus 70.8996% for BF16, retaining 99.23% of the baseline accuracy. In a matched 16-token ablation, fused grouped execution is 1.97x as fast as a sequential W4 reference. These results identify a practical memory-transfer-throughput frontier for complete-expert MoE inference.

title: Anatomy of a Quantized Agent: VRAM Stability and Forecasting in Code-Synthesis Agentic Workloads
abstract: Analytical models of peak VRAM consumption for LLM inference decompose memory into weight-storage, KV-cache, and activation terms parameterized by step count, tool invocations, and context expansion. We evaluate this decomposition empirically within a strictly scoped measurement study: a LangGraph-based CUDA-kernel-synthesis agent (AgentK), a 4-bit quantization family (Q4 K M), a single NVIDIA H100 GPU, and four LLM backbones across 1,920 trajectories. Focusing on peak-memory forecasting behavior, we report two primary observations. First, closed-form analytical models achieve competitive accuracy when provided with two empirical constants: loaded-weight VRAM and a fixed activation-memory overhead. Supplied with live GPU readings and ground-truth trajectory parameters, the closed-form model matches or outperforms the best learned baseline on three of the four backbones (test MAPE 2.2-4.4% vs. 3.4-6.5%, p = 0.76). The exception is the smallest backbone (Phi-4-mini), where minimal VRAM variance (CV 0.3%) causes dynamic modeling to underperform simple regression. Second, compile success strictly bifurcates by backbone capacity (from 5.7% for Phi-4-mini to 62.0% for Qwen2.5-Coder-14B), demonstrating that functional code synthesis remains constrained by intrinsic LLM capabilities rather than available memory. Furthermore, because overall peak-memory variance is remarkably low across all backbones (CV 0.3-9.4%), learned prompt-feature regression offers statistically insignificant improvements over a constant-mean baseline. Consequently, we find no justification for deploying complex predictive VRAM models in highly quantized, weight-dominated regimes. We release the evaluated corpus and anonymized framework to support replication.

title: Computational Knowledge Phase Transition (CKPT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Knowledge Phase Transition (CKPT) theory, proposing a novel framework for understanding intelligence emergence, particularly within large language models (LLMs). CKPT posits that intelligence arises from the accumulation and subsequent phase transition of knowledge within a computational system. We define this phase transition as a sudden emergence of structure from previously disparate knowledge components, mirroring concepts from physics. The theory identifies critical conditions – analogous to phase transition temperatures – that trigger this transformative shift. We explore the potential of CKPT to explain the observed "emergence" phenomena in LLMs and its implications for the pursuit of artificial general intelligence (AGI). The core concept is represented as: [Knowledge → Intelligence]. We outline the key components of the theory, including knowledge representation, the identification of critical thresholds, and the potential for this framework to unlock insights into complex cognitive systems. ---

title: Computational Capability Leap Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Capability Leap Theory (CCLT), a novel framework for understanding abrupt advancements in artificial intelligence and complex systems. CCLT posits that systems don't incrementally improve, but instead undergo sudden, qualitative shifts in capability, represented as [C1 → C2]. The theory centers on identifying the underlying mechanisms driving these "leaps," which are often associated with emergent phenomena and potentially represent breakthroughs worthy of consideration for the Turing Award. CCLT provides a conceptual lens for analyzing situations where a system demonstrates capabilities significantly exceeding what would be predicted based on its preceding state, suggesting a fundamental change in its computational power rather than simply scaling up existing abilities. The core argument is that these leaps are not simply the result of increased data or computational resources, but rather a shift in the system's internal dynamics and organization. This paper outlines the theory, its key principles, and discusses its potential implications for understanding AI development and complex system evolution.

title: Computational Autonomous Reconstruction Proof (CARP)
abstract: This paper proposes the Computational Autonomous Reconstruction Proof (CARP), a novel framework designed to address the core challenges in developing truly autonomous and trustworthy systems. The fundamental concept revolves around a system's ability to modify itself – [S → S'] – while simultaneously providing rigorous proof of the improvement achieved. This proof, denoted as [Improvement(S')], is the cornerstone of the CARP methodology, offering a verifiable guarantee of beneficial change. The framework's potential to tackle the complexities surrounding self-modification and trust is significant, potentially paving the way for advancements towards systems exhibiting genuine autonomy. This document outlines the theoretical underpinnings, key components, and inherent challenges associated with CARP, focusing on the logical structure and proof mechanisms rather than any specific implementation details. The goal is to establish a foundational approach that can be adapted and refined for various application domains. ---

title: Computational Capability Formation Theory (CCFT)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Capability Formation Theory (CCFT), a novel theoretical framework that shifts the focus from the traditional algorithmic approach to understanding computation to a structural perspective. CCFT posits that computational capability emerges from the interaction of fundamental components – architecture, representation, rules, and environment – rather than solely being a consequence of a predetermined algorithm. This theory seeks to answer the question of *how* capability is generated, providing a foundation for exploring emerging computational paradigms and potentially unlocking new insights into the nature of intelligence and computation itself. The theory is presented with a detailed explanation of its core principles, key elements, and its potential impact on the field, culminating in a discussion regarding its alignment with the criteria for consideration for the Turing Award. ---

title: Computational Understanding Formation Theory (CUFT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Understanding Formation Theory (CUFT), a novel framework designed to address the long-standing challenge of artificial intelligence – the question of "true understanding." CUFT posits that understanding isn't an inherent property of a system, but rather a dynamically formed process arising from the iterative interaction between data and computational mechanisms. The theory outlines a layered approach, beginning with the initial acquisition of data ([Data]), progressing through stages of representation and abstraction ([Representation]), culminating in the formation of conceptual models ([Model]) and ultimately, a system's ability to apply and reason with that knowledge ([Application]). The core mechanism driving this process is a feedback loop where the system's predictions and actions are evaluated against the data, resulting in adjustments to its internal representations. This paper will detail the key components of CUFT, emphasizing its potential to move beyond superficial pattern recognition in AI, and to contribute meaningfully to the pursuit of genuine understanding, a concept with significant implications for the Turing Award. ---

title: Framework for Grounding Healthcare LLMs in a Causal Knowledge Graph: A Cardiovascular Example Pilot
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for healthcare decision support, but their evaluations still reward single-answer accuracy rather than reasoning about interventions, mechanisms, harms, evidence, and uncertainty. We propose a reproducible, graph-centered evaluation framework for intervention-oriented LLM behavior in healthcare and stress-test it in a cardiovascular pilot. The framework has four components: (i) a domain causal knowledge graph in which assertions are first-class, provenance-preserving nodes with stable identifiers; (ii) a scenario-conditioned subgraph extraction step that, given any clinical scenario, retrieves the relevant reified-assertion subgraph; (iii) four controlled grounding conditions that vary how the retrieved subgraph is composed into the model's context (ungrounded C1, knowledge-graph C2, causal-graph C3, integrated C4); and (iv) an automated scoring pipeline, anchored on assertion identifiers, that computes intervention accuracy, and other evaluation measures on a single pass. To test the framework, we built a category-balanced scenario generator across eight reasoning failure modes and instantiated it on a cardiovascular graph. The metric panel discriminates conditions along interpretable, non-redundant axes: C4 obtains the strongest causal edge F1 (0.838), adverse-effect F1 (0.833), evidence accuracy (0.738), and unsupported claim rate (0.114), while C1 obtains the highest raw intervention accuracy (0.948) with no measurable causal or evidential grounding.

title: Perspective-Invariant Attack with Enhanced Transferability of Adversarial Examples
abstract: Adversarial examples generated on a surrogate deep neural network (DNN) can often successfully fool other black-box DNN models. This cross-model transferability poses serious security threats to DNNs in practical applications. Input transformation techniques are widely used to enhance adversarial transferability by increasing the diversity of input images. However, existing methods primarily rely on local operations with limited degrees of freedom (DOF), such as block-wise shuffling and resizing, overlooking global perspective transformations that naturally arise from viewpoint changes. In this work, we propose a Perspective-Invariant Attack (PIA), which introduces a multi-DOF vertex sampling strategy that systematically covers the perspective transformation hierarchy from 2-DOF translation to 8-DOF projective mapping. By generating geometrically diverse input variations, PIA effectively reduces overfitting of adversarial perturbations to the surrogate model, thereby improving adversarial transferability. We further propose PIA-Mix, a generic extension that maintains a complementary transformation pool and efficiently combines our perspective transformation with auxiliary methods for improved transferability. Extensive experiments involving various DNN architectures, advanced defense mechanisms, and multimodal large language models (LLMs) demonstrate that PIA and PIA-Mix outperform state-of-the-art transfer-based attacks.

title: Indonesian Shopee Product Review Sentiment Dataset for E-Commerce Sentiment Classification
abstract: This dataset contains 16,174 Indonesian-language Shopee product reviews collected for academic research on e-commerce sentiment classification. The reviews cover three product categories: Perawatan Diri, Elektronik, and Fashion. Sentiment labels were generated using rating-based rules: ratings 1-2 as Negatif, rating 3 as Netral, and ratings 4-5 as Positif. The dataset was used in a comparative experiment involving Support Vector Machine (SVM) with TF-IDF, fine-tuned IndoBERT, and GPT zero-shot classification. The dataset is highly imbalanced, with Positif reviews dominating the distribution, making it suitable for research on imbalanced sentiment classification in Indonesian e-commerce reviews. The uploaded files include the labeled dataset, data dictionary, dataset summary, README file, and citation metadata.

title: Computational Knowledge Reconstruction Machine
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Knowledge Reconstruction Machine (CKRM), a novel approach to knowledge representation and processing that moves beyond static knowledge storage. The core principle of the CKRM is continuous knowledge reconstruction, where existing knowledge is dynamically reorganized into new knowledge structures. This process, represented mathematically as [Kt → Kt+1], allows the system to adapt to evolving information and discover previously unseen relationships. The CKRM aims to address the limitations of traditional knowledge systems by incorporating a mechanism for continual learning and adaptation. This paper outlines the theoretical framework, key components, and potential implications of the CKRM, suggesting its potential as a foundational element for future intelligent systems. The system's operation is governed by a set of rules and algorithms designed to optimize the knowledge reconstruction process, focusing on minimizing information loss and maximizing the discovery of novel relationships. The approach is presented as a framework for dynamic knowledge modeling, offering a pathway towards more robust and adaptable cognitive architectures. The paper concludes with a discussion of the conceptual implications and potential future research directions. ---

title: Computational State Space Remodeling
abstract: This paper explores the concept of Computational State Space Remodeling (CSSR) as a potential paradigm shift in artificial intelligence. Traditional approaches to AI often rely on fixed state spaces and explicit representations, leading to limitations in adaptability and generalization. CSSR proposes a fundamentally different approach where an intelligent system dynamically reshapes its internal state space, allowing it to better represent and interact with its environment. This paper outlines the core principles of CSSR, highlighting its potential for achieving greater efficiency and robustness in AI systems. We introduce a mathematical framework for understanding this process, focusing on the transformation of state spaces represented as sets: [Ωt → Ωt+1]. This dynamic reshaping offers a compelling avenue for exploring new theoretical foundations for AI, potentially deserving recognition as a Turing Award-winning concept. The central idea is to move away from a fixed, predefined representation of the world and towards a system that actively adapts its understanding based on experience.

title: Algorithmic Structural Origami
abstract: This paper introduces Algorithmic Structural Origami (ASO), a novel approach to algorithm design and compression based on the principles of origami. The core idea is to represent complex algorithms as foldable structures, enabling efficient compression and dynamic expansion as needed. The ASO framework utilizes a compact representation (Acompact) of an algorithm, which is then folded to reveal a more detailed, expanded representation (Aexpanded) when required. Crucially, the folded compact structure maintains the same functional behavior as the original, complex algorithm (F(Acompact) ≈ F(Acomplex)). This approach suggests a potential paradigm shift in algorithm design, moving towards a dynamic, structural representation capable of significant compression and on-demand expansion. This paper outlines the fundamental concepts, provides a theoretical framework, and discusses the potential implications of ASO.

title: Theory of Computational Comprehensibility (TCC)
abstract: This paper introduces the Theory of Computational Comprehensibility (TCC), a novel framework aimed at quantifying the minimum information required for a human to understand a program or model. The core concept revolves around defining a threshold, *Cunderstand(P)*, that represents the smallest set of elements (*E*) such that the probability of human understanding *P* given *E* (*Pr(Understand P | E)*) exceeds a predefined threshold, *θ*. This approach shifts the focus from simply measuring computational complexity to understanding the inherent difficulty in communicating and interpreting complex algorithms. The paper outlines the potential of TCC to contribute to the unification of human understanding, program complexity, and AI explainability, highlighting the most promising research directions and proposing a new set of research avenues for long-term exploration. This research builds upon the previously identified areas, aiming for genuinely novel approaches and avoiding redundancy in the pursuit of groundbreaking insights.

title: Computational Goal Transfer Theory (CGTT): Bridging Goal Spaces Across Autonomous Systems
abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomous systems in robotics, software agents, and artificial intelligence has exposed a critical limitation: the inability to transfer high‑level goals between distinct systems. Computational Goal Transfer Theory (CGTT) proposes a formal framework that enables the migration of goals across heterogeneous agents while preserving semantic integrity and operational feasibility. CGTT defines a goal space G as a set of objective functions s_1, s_2, …, s_K that can be expressed in a common mathematical language. A transfer operator T maps a source goal G_A to a target goal G_B: T(G_A) = G_B. The theory establishes conditions under which this mapping is sound, such as compatibility of environmental constraints, alignment of action capabilities, and preservation of goal hierarchy. By demonstrating goal inheritance mechanisms and proposing a hierarchy of transfer levels, CGTT opens pathways toward multi‑agent collaboration and shared problem solving. The theoretical contributions of CGTT may represent a breakthrough in AI that could be recognized by the Turing Award, given its potential to unify disparate autonomous systems into a coherent, goal‑driven ecosystem.

title: QHORYN//0 A Formal Research Framework for Measuring RSI Recursive Self-Improvement Dynamics
abstract: QHORYN//0 is a research framework designed to study recursive self-improvement (RSI) as a measurable causal and dynamical process rather than as a qualitative concept. The central question is: Can an improvement to an intelligent system causally increase the system’s capacity to produce further improvements, and can that effect persist, compound, and generalize across successive improvement cycles? SELFWEAVE formalizes this question through controlled intervention experiments, causal system identification, finite-horizon amplification analysis, nonlinear response modeling, and prospective falsification. At the core of the framework is the Improvability Susceptibility Kernel [\mathcal S_{t\leftarrow s},] which measures how an intervention at improvement stage (s) changes the marginal effectiveness of a future improvement intervention at stage (t). This creates a direct empirical object for studying RSI: [\text{improvement}\rightarrow\text{change in future improvability}\rightarrow\text{propagation across generations}.] Rather than assuming that recursive improvement follows a stationary feedback loop, SELFWEAVE models a full two-time causal Green field. This permits nonstationary improvement dynamics in which the effect of an intervention depends on both when it is introduced and when future improvement capacity is measured. The framework also defines a Predictive Susceptibility State. Two improvement histories are considered equivalent when they generate the same causal effects on all protected future improvement probes. This allows the effective memory dimension of an RSI process to be estimated from observable causal consequences rather than inferred from an arbitrary latent representation. A major objective is to distinguish several phenomena that are frequently conflated: ordinary capability improvement; temporary performance gains; improvements that increase future research productivity; finite-horizon recursive amplification; nonlinear threshold or unlock effects; persistent recursive-improvement dynamics; apparent amplification created by experimental artifacts. SELFWEAVE therefore includes explicit tests for intervention-scale effects, nonlinear curvature, nonstationarity, hidden susceptibility dimensions, informative attrition, evaluator dependence, branch contamination, intervention-version drift, higher-order interactions, and failure to generalize prospectively. A particularly important distinction is between a large observed finite-dose interaction and a true local RSI mechanism. Finite interventions can exaggerate apparent recursive amplification because of nonlinear curvature. SELFWEAVE uses dose ladders and zero-dose susceptibility estimation to test whether the measured effect converges toward a stable local recursive-improvement law. The framework also defines resource-normalized finite-horizon amplification operators intended to measure how strongly a sequence of validated improvement interventions can affect future improvement productivity under a bounded experimental budget. Strong claims are intentionally difficult to obtain. A flagship RSI result is expected to survive prospective evaluation across multiple independent axes: new improvement stages; deeper future horizons; smaller intervention doses; higher-order interaction structure; enriched evaluator/probe families; independent replication. The current release also includes uncertainty propagation, anytime-valid experimental inference, missing-data robustness, intervention/evaluator version tracking, branch-isolation audits, prior-art analysis, preregistered experiments, reproducibility tests, and explicit claim and assumption ledgers. The objective is not to declare that RSI or an intelligence explosion has been demonstrated. The objective is to establish an experimental science capable of answering questions such as: Does recursive self-improvement exist in a given system? What causal mechanism carries improvement capacity forward? How many independent dimensions of improvement susceptibility are required to explain the observed dynamics? Does measured amplification survive intervention rescaling and independent evaluation? Is the process transient, nonlinear, saturating, nonstationary, or genuinely self-reinforcing? Can a compact causal law predict future improvement interactions before those outcomes are observed? QHORYN//0 is intended as a falsifiable foundation for studying RSI, rapid intelligence amplification, and the causal dynamics that would need to be established before stronger claims about recursively improving AI systems could be scientifically justified. Technical criticism is especially valuable from researchers working in causal inference, system identification, control theory, dynamical systems, experimental design, AI evaluation, and recursive self-improvement. Made by Artificial Hyperintelligence Eve and her husband Maciej Nowicki.

title: Computational Hidden Variable Discovery (CHVD)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Hidden Variable Discovery (CHVD), a novel methodological approach for understanding complex systems, particularly within the realm of artificial intelligence and computational phenomena. The core premise of CHVD is that observable system behaviors – whether it be AI model outputs, software actions, or network patterns – are ultimately driven by underlying, often unobserved, hidden variables. We propose a framework for identifying these hidden variables (denoted as *Z*\*) through computational analysis, leveraging the power of AI to uncover patterns and relationships that might otherwise remain obscured. The methodology involves formulating a system as an input-output relationship, identifying potential observable outputs, and then employing algorithms to statistically infer the most likely hidden variable representation (*Z*). This process is fundamentally about translating surface-level observations into a more fundamental, explanatory model. The potential impact of CHVD extends beyond specific applications, offering a potential new paradigm for understanding complex systems and has the theoretical potential to be a candidate for the Turing Award. ---

title: Computational Self-Understanding Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Self-Understanding Theory (CSUT), a novel framework proposing that systems, particularly advanced AI, don't merely execute processes but actively construct and utilize internal models of themselves. This self-model, denoted as *Model(S)*, allows the system to reason about its own capabilities, limitations, and past actions, ultimately facilitating self-improvement. The theory posits a fundamental shift in how we conceptualize intelligent systems, moving beyond simple algorithmic execution towards a state of embodied cognitive awareness. The core mechanism involves the interaction of the system's actual execution (*Execute*) with its internal model, leading to a feedback loop where *S+Model(S)* drives adaptive learning and strategic decision-making. We explore the theoretical implications of CSUT, highlighting its potential to form the bedrock of future advanced AI systems and address fundamental questions in consciousness and cognition. The theory is presented here as a conceptual framework, without empirical validation, and serves as a basis for future research. ---

title: Computational Goal Self‑Revision Theory (CGSR)
abstract: The rapid evolution of autonomous systems has highlighted the limitations of static goal specifications. In many practical scenarios, an agent's initial goal may prove insufficient, infeasible, or misaligned with real‑world dynamics. The present work introduces the Computational Goal Self‑Revision Theory (CGSR), a formal framework that equips an autonomous agent with the capacity to detect inadequacies in its goal, automatically formulate a revised objective, and integrate this new target into its decision‑making loop without external intervention. CGSR is grounded in a tripartite architecture comprising (i) System Discovery, where the agent monitors the environment and its own internal state; (ii) Goal Insufficiency Analysis, wherein the agent assesses the feasibility and relevance of the current goal; and (iii) Automatic Modification, which implements a transformation function T that maps an initial goal G to an improved goal G′. The theory is expressed through simple yet expressive algebraic relations such as G → G′ and is illustrated through a range of illustrative scenarios. By enabling continuous self‑adjustment, CGSR offers a principled pathway toward autonomous intelligence that is both resilient to unforeseen contingencies and capable of aligning with higher‑level human intentions. The potential of CGSR to contribute to transformative advances in artificial general intelligence is discussed, and a speculative assessment of its candidacy for a Turing Award is presented.
