title: ORCID: 0009-0005-1860-0009
abstract: Computational Knowledge Reconstruction Theory (CKRT) proposes a principled framework for deriving hidden knowledge structures from observable results in complex systems. By formalizing the relationship between observations and underlying knowledge through a bidirectional mapping, CKRT enables the reconstruction of internal states that are not directly measurable. The theory introduces the concept of result recovery, whereby the final output of a system can be inverted to reveal the sequence of knowledge states that produced it. Hidden knowledge structures are captured as latent variables within a structured probabilistic model, allowing for the systematic exploration of knowledge dynamics. CKRT also highlights the potential of this approach to contribute to the design of systems that emulate human-like understanding and to the advancement of computational theory at the level recognized by prestigious awards such as the Turing Award. The following paper elaborates the theoretical foundations, formal model, and implications of CKRT for understanding complex systems and guiding future research in knowledge representation and inference.

title: Second-Order Policy Effects as State Transitions: A Source-Linked Benchmark for Policy Simulation
abstract: Policy evaluation often estimates direct benefits and costs while treating the institutional environment as fixed. In practice, a policy changes the system it enters: actors adapt, enforcement capacity shifts, burdens move, and new equilibria form around capture, gaming, compliance theater, irreversibility, and repair costs. We formalize this as second-order policy-effect prediction and present a source-linked benchmark for policy simulation. The benchmark contains 96 named public-policy cases across eight domains and four balanced action classes: implement, modify, pilot, and block. Each case includes source locators and state variables for benefit, capture, gaming, burden shift, instability, uncertainty, irreversibility, distributional risk, and implementation capacity. The runner regenerates method outputs and aggregate results from the case table, and the simulator never reads the expert action target. We report a protocol-based transition-channel audit with recall, precision, F1-style efficiency, and selective top-channel stress diagnostics, so universal channel coverage is not mistaken for field validation. The side-effect simulator achieves mean policy-effect quality of 0.945, compared with 0.838 for the risk-register baseline and 0.879 for the causal-loop baseline. Its advantage is concentrated in side-effect recall and aggregate transition scoring; it does not dominate the best structured baselines on exact policy-action choice. The evidence remains benchmark-based, but supports a bounded claim: transition-state variables make policy simulators more sensitive to downstream institutional effects.

title: An Agentic Framework for Financial Disclosure Intelligence
abstract: An Agentic Framework for Financial Disclosure Intelligence TREO Talk Paper Kazim Topuz, Ph.D. The University of Tulsa kazim-topuz@utulsa.edu Tally Ferguson The University of Tulsa tally-ferguson@utulsa.edu Jessica Bedson The University of Tulsa jab1664@utulsa.edu Abstract Corporate disclosures in SEC 10-K filings are one of the most prevalent ways firms communicate forward-looking risk to investors, yet analytical methods for reviewing these disclosures have developed independently of one another. We introduce an agentic framework for financial disclosure intelligence in which lexicon-based and transformer-based models function as cooperative agents rather than opposing alternatives. The framework is applied to 10-K filings from a sample of 55 large-cap firms across all 11 GICS sectors from 2016 to 2025. From each filing, we extract the Risk Factors (Item 1A) and Management Discussion and Analysis (Item 7) sections and score paragraph-level tone using both the Loughran-McDonald dictionary and FinBERT. We also introduce a multi-layer validation design that addresses the absence of universal "ground truth" labels in financial disclosure text. We then examine systematic patterns of disagreement between the dictionary and transformer models to identify cases of contextual ambiguity, boilerplate language reuse, and legal hedging. Results show strong directional agreement between the two models in identifying positive and negative tone across firms and sectors, with clear differences in sensitivity. FinBERT produces a more extensive range of scores, while the Loughran-McDonald dictionary provides stable, interpretable readings at scale. The study contributes to information systems research by presenting a modular, extensible architecture for disclosure analytics that can incorporate additional agents, such as a large language model adjudication layer, without requiring redesign of the underlying system. Our agentic LLM agent approach should more comprehensively recognize how specific combinations of phrases disclosed in financial statements portend positive, negative, or neutral outlooks. Implementing such a system offers the potential to refine financial instrument valuation and enhance the precision of regulatory oversight and compliance monitoring. References Araci, D. (2019). FinBERT: Financial sentiment analysis with pre-trained language models. arXiv preprint arXiv:1908.10063. https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10063 Loughran, T., & McDonald, B. (2011). When is a liability not a liability? Textual analysis, dictionaries, and 10-Ks. Journal of Finance, 66(1), 35–65.

title: Consequence Type System
abstract: This paper introduces the Consequence Type System (CTS), a novel approach to type checking that extends traditional type systems by explicitly modeling the potential consequences of operations. Unlike conventional type systems which primarily focus on static shape analysis, CTS adds annotations to operations indicating the possible effects they may induce, categorized as StateChange, ResourceUse, and ExternalEffect. This allows compilers to perform runtime checks to verify whether a program's execution will result in undesirable long-term consequences. The CTS offers a pathway to significantly enhance software safety and improve the reliability of AI tool calls by providing a more comprehensive understanding of potential operational impacts. This system has the potential to revolutionize type theory and offer a powerful framework for building more robust and secure software systems. ---

title: MULTI-FUSE: Multimodal Late Fusion Framework for Hate Speech Detection in Videos
authors: Lekshmi M S and Malathy S
abstract: Abstract Addressing cyberbullying and fostering more welcoming online communities depend on the detection of hateful content. However, because it requires examin-ing a number of interrelated components, including spoken words, visual imagery, and text within those visuals, detecting hate speech in videos is difficult. Thiswork presents MULTI-FUSE, a state-of-the-art hate speech detection model thatsuccessfully combines multimodal features from video content using a late fusion technique. The audio and video frames are processed separately by the frame-work. It analyzes frames for hate symbols, text (using OCR), and gestures to generate a visual hate score using deep learning techniques, while extractingand analyzing speech to generate an audio hate score. These audio and visualhate scores are then combined into a single feature vector, which is input into asupervised learning classifier for the final prediction of hate speech. This studypresents an optimized multimodal framework for detecting hate speech in videos by assessing various supervised learning models and identifying the Support Vec-tor Machine (SVM) as the most effective classifier, achieving an accuracy of 0.8571, precision of 0.8333, recall of 0.8929, and F1-score of 0.8621. The frame-work systematically determines the optimal frame-processing rate of one frame per second to strike a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. Anablation study confirms that the full multimodal combination (audio, text, andvisual) significantly outperforms all unimodal configurations, achieving a 7.5%relative improvement over the best unimodal model. Compared with reportedbaselines on the HATEMM dataset, MULTI-FUSE achieves an 18% improvementin F1-score over existing late-fusion approaches. The late fusion method mergesaudio, text, and visual hate scores, resulting in strong detection performance

title: Computational Experience Fusion Theory (CEFT-2)
abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomous systems and intelligent agents has resulted in a vast accumulation of experiential data across diverse domains. Yet, each system typically processes its own experience in isolation, limiting the potential for collective intelligence. This paper introduces Computational Experience Fusion Theory (CEFT-2), a formal framework that defines a systematic fusion operation for experiential knowledge, denoted as E_1 + E_2 → E_3, where E_i represents the experiential state of system i. By iteratively applying this operation across a network of agents, CEFT-2 constructs a hierarchy of aggregated experiences, culminating in collective computational wisdom. We formalize the fusion operation, explore its algebraic properties, and demonstrate how CEFT-2 can serve as a foundational theory for future group AI systems. The paper argues that CEFT-2 embodies the principles that could underpin a Turing Award–level contribution, providing a scalable, interpretable, and ethically grounded approach to multi-agent knowledge integration.

title: Computational Experience Compression Theory (CECT)
abstract: The proliferation of data generated by modern computing systems has created an unprecedented opportunity to capture and reuse the knowledge embedded in large collections of run histories. Computational Experience Compression Theory (CECT) proposes a principled framework for transforming extensive execution logs into compact symbolic representations, referred to as Experience Codes. By encoding the essential patterns of successful and failed executions, CECT enables downstream systems to perform expert‑level judgments in a fraction of the time required for traditional simulation or exhaustive search. This paper develops the theoretical foundations of CECT, formalizes the encoding and decoding processes, and demonstrates how the resulting Experience Codes can be leveraged for rapid decision making in diverse domains such as program synthesis, automated debugging, and adaptive resource management. We further discuss the implications of CECT for the broader field of artificial intelligence, highlighting its potential to elucidate the mechanisms underlying machine expertise and to guide the design of next‑generation autonomous systems.

title: ENAF: A Multi-Exit Network with an Adaptive Patch Fusion for Large Image Super Resolution
abstract: To accelerate single image super-resolution (SISR) networks on large images (2K-8K), many recent approaches decompose an image into small patches and dynamically determine an execution path according to its difficulty (referred to as a dynamic network). To quantify the hardness of a patch, they mainly rely on a handcrafted assessment score, e.g., edge, which weakly associates a patch's texture with the computational complexity of a SISR model. To address the problem, we introduce ENAF - a dynamic network for SISR with an adaptive patch fusion. Built on top of a backbone, ENAF incorporates multiple early exits (EEs) to tackle the over-parameterized SISR model. More importantly, ENAF plugs a tiny network that estimates PSNR to associate data texture with a computation cost at an EE. Based on the scores, ENAF effectively assigns image patches to an exit, enhancing the quality-complexity trade-off. Extensive experiments on common datasets with popular SISR backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of ENAF in various settings. The source code is provided in https://github.com/nmduonggg/ENAF

title: MODAL: Multi-Modal Object Re-ID via Model-Driven Sparse Decoupling and Text-Image Differential Filtering
abstract: Multi-modal object re-identification (Re-ID) aims to facilitate cross-camera object retrieval in complex environments by leveraging complementary information from visual (e.g., RGB, NIR, TIR) and textual modalities. However, existing approaches often lack principled feature disentanglement and coherent multi-modal integration, leading to entangled representations that introduce cross-modal conflicts, obscure discriminative cues, and suffer distribution shift under modality-missing conditions. To tackle these challenges, we propose MODAL, a novel multi-modal object re-identification framework, grounded in coupled sparse coding theory and differential suppression principles. A core component of MODAL is a Multi-modal Feature Sparse Decoupling module, developed in a model-driven deep unrolling manner based on multi-modal coupled sparse coding. It explicitly decomposes multi-modal features into uni-modal specific, bi-modal and tri-modal shared representations, thereby achieving more transparent and effective feature disentanglement. Benefiting from the principled feature disentanglement, MODAL naturally mitigates performance degradation in incomplete-modality scenarios via a Modality-Aware Subspace Activation that selectively activates only the consistently shared subspaces. Moreover, we propose a Text-Image Differential Filtering module that leverages coarse-grained textual semantics to adaptively suppress task-irrelevant responses in the decoupled visual representations, thereby enhancing discriminative information. Extensive experiments on four datasets demonstrate that MODAL achieves state-of-the-art performance with superior transparency.

title: Can Boredom be Computational? A Functional Idle-state Mechanism for Reflective Cognition in AI Agents
abstract: AI is known for its enablement of machines to mimic human brains when performing tasks (PK, 1984). We discuss the concept of boredom-inspired reflective agency for autonomous AI systems. Existing agentic architecture prioritizes continuous optimization and task execution. With more human-like designs of AI agents, anthropomorphic agents not only can reason, but can show emotions and develop personality traits (Alabed et al., 2022). However, unlike humans, AI systems steer off topics with language complexities and little context causing a ‘conversational drift’ (Armstrong et al., 2025; Namala, 2024). To mitigate this problem, AI agents can engage in internal cognitive processes that revisit past decisions, evaluate successful and unsuccessful outcomes, simulate alternative scenarios, consolidate memories, and anticipate future actions. This can happen during periods of inactivity to overcome boredom. Rather than acquiring new external knowledge, we ask the question of whether the system should reflect on judgement and strategically self-assess similar to human introspection during idle moments. The TREO argues that reflective idle cognition may represent a missing architectural layer in agentic AI, enabling more context-aware, adaptive, and strategically coherent autonomous behavior. Human boredom may not be wasted cognition. It may be an evolutionary mechanism for reflective simulation, emotional replay, memory consolidation, and future planning. Current agentic AI systems lack this reflective idle architecture. Adding this layer to its architecture would contribute to the debate of whether anthropomorphism is actually a hype (Placani, 2024). The proposed framework conceptualizes boredom as a productive reflective state. This topic inherently presents an interesting interdisciplinary TREO that includes systems design, psychology, cognitive science and AI

title: Trustworthy in silico labeling via semantic visual interpretability of image-to-image translation
abstract: Abstract Cross-modality image translation promises to provide multiple layers of biological information from a single image input, yet its practical application is stalled by a lack of interpretability and the inability to account for model imperfections. In silico labeling, the inference of organelle localization from label-free images, is a primary example where this black-box nature limits adoption. We present Mask Interpreter, a generalized method for semantic visual interpretability of image-to-image translation models. By uncovering organelle-specific “explanation signatures”, Mask Interpreter validates that models rely on authentic biological structures rather than spurious artifacts. Beyond biological validation, it outperforms traditional explainable AI (xAI) approaches, identifies batch effects and localizes prediction errors when ground-truth fluorescence is unavailable. Semantic confidence modeling further provides fine-grained reliability assessment at single-cell resolution, enabling the automated exclusion of artifacts from downstream analyses. By bridging the gap between computational inference and meaningful biological features, Mask Interpreter transforms in silico labeling into a reliable tool for scientific discovery across diverse biomedical imaging modalities.

title: Persistent Behavioral Signatures in Large Language Models: A Three-Replicate Baseline Test of Representational Persistence
abstract: This study examines whether large language models exhibit stable, model-specific representational patterns across repeated independent trials. Eleven AI systems were tested using the same standardized environment and self-representation prompts across three baseline replicates, producing 66 formal observations. Eight locally hosted model configurations were tested under controlled settings with tools, web access, retrieval, memory, file context, and custom system prompts disabled. Three hosted systems were tested in fresh conversations under documented platform-controlled conditions. The study extends earlier exploratory work by testing whether differences between models persist rather than appearing only once. Responses were coded for dimensions including embodiment, anthropomorphism, abstraction, relational orientation, self-environment differentiation, and recurring symbolic motifs. Across the three replicates, responses generated by the same model were substantially more similar to one another than responses generated by different models. Mean within-model similarity was 0.898 compared with 0.679 between models. The difference was statistically significant and large in magnitude. The findings support the concept of a Model-Specific Response Signature: a recurring configuration of generated response features that remains distinguishable across independent trials. The study also identifies a distinction between stable representational structure and variable surface imagery, showing that models can change metaphors while retaining deeper patterns of organization, embodiment, boundary, and relational orientation. The research does not interpret these signatures as evidence of consciousness, subjective experience, or human personality. Instead, it establishes a reproducible framework for studying persistent model-specific representational behavior. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21961915

title: Computational Memory Selection Theory (CMST)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Memory Selection Theory (CMST), a novel framework for understanding and designing intelligent systems. CMST posits that intelligent agents do not necessarily retain and process *all* historical data encountered. Instead, the theory proposes that agents strategically select a subset of this data – denoted as [Memory^*] – to retain and utilize, based on a defined selection criteria. The core of CMST lies in understanding *what* historical information is deemed 'worth' preserving and *how* this selection process impacts the agent's decision-making capabilities. This approach offers a potentially significant shift in how we conceptualize memory within artificial intelligence, with implications for future AI architectures and potentially aligning with the criteria for recognition as a Turing Award winner. The theory is presented as a foundational framework, focusing on the conceptual and theoretical aspects, without requiring experimental validation. ---

evidence.abstract: This paper introduces Computational Memory Selection Theory (CMST), a novel framework for understanding and designing intelligent systems. CMST posits that intelligent agents do not necessarily retain and process *all* historical data encountered. Instead, the theory proposes that agents strategically select a subset of this data – denoted as [Memory^*] – to retain and utilize, based on a defined selection criteria. The core of CMST lies in understanding *what* historical information is deemed 'worth' preserving and *how* this selection process impacts the agent's decision-making capabilities. This approach offers a potentially significant shift in how we conceptualize memory within artificial intelligence, with implications for future AI architectures and potentially aligning with the criteria for recognition as a Turing Award winner. The theory is presented as a foundational framework, focusing on the conceptual and theoretical aspects, without requiring experimental validation. ---

title: Computational Information Transformation Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Information Transformation Theory (CITT), a novel theoretical framework designed to comprehensively analyze the processes of information conversion across diverse formats. CITT posits that every information transformation, regardless of its underlying mechanism, involves a complex interplay of preservation, loss, and generation of information. The theory is built upon the core concept of mapping between information instances: [I1 → I2], where I1 and I2 represent information in different forms. The central focus is to systematically investigate the transformations occurring during this conversion, detailing what aspects are retained, what is inevitably lost, and what entirely new information is produced. CITT aims to provide a unified theoretical foundation for information computation, potentially holding the key to unlocking advancements in areas such as artificial intelligence, data science, and cryptography. The theory's underlying mathematical framework is presented, laying the groundwork for further research and development. ---

title: Unified Computational Goal Theory (UCGT)
abstract: Computational systems have historically focused on three core questions: how to compute, how to store, and how to learn. However, the emergence of advanced artificial intelligence and autonomous agents demands a new theoretical foundation that explains why a system chooses to act in a particular way. Unified Computational Goal Theory (UCGT) proposes a comprehensive framework that unifies optimization goals, biological goals, artificial intelligence goals, multi‑agent goals, and social goals within a single mathematical structure. By formalizing the relationship between environment, memory, capability, goal, and action, UCGT provides a principled method for deriving goals from first principles, thereby offering a potential next generation of theoretical underpinnings for artificial intelligence. This paper presents the core ideas of UCGT, its mathematical formalization, illustrative models, and implications for future research in AI, multi‑agent systems, and computational cognition.

title: The New AI Architect: Composing Intelligence Through AI Technology Stacks
abstract: AI is no longer just something organizations adopt, it is something they must design. As firms assemble models, data, and workflows into interconnected systems, the challenge shifts from using AI tools to composing intelligence. This panel introduces the concept of the AI Architect, a role focused on integrating AI capabilities into coherent, scalable solutions that support organizational objectives. Panelists will examine how these systems are structured, how they reshape decision-making and work processes, and why they represent a new phase of digital transformation. The discussion also addresses the risks of this shift, including security vulnerabilities, misuse, and governance challenges that emerge in highly integrated environments. By bringing together perspectives from research and practice, the panel highlights emerging directions for Information Systems scholarship in understanding and managing AI-enabled organizations.

title: Operational Identifiability of Tensor Product Structures: Exact Rigidity Laws, a Two-Operation Threshold, and an Aliasing Limit
abstract: Here's what this paper means for actual humans: WHAT THIS IS ABOUT. When you build or use a quantum device, everything rests on knowing what its parts are: which degrees of freedom are "qubit 1," which are "qubit 2." The companion paper ("Forged Frames") showed that simple mathematical criteria cannot certify this; convincing fakes exist. This paper answers the question that result leaves standing: what is the MINIMUM experimental information that genuinely pins down a system's subsystem structure, and when can that information silently fail? WHAT WE FOUND, IN PLAIN TERMS. Four things. (1) EXACT LAWS INSTEAD OF MEASUREMENTS. Any wrong choice of parts must visibly distort the family of unentangled states, and we derive exactly how much, at every system size: closed-form constants (verified to seven decimal places), an explicit error bound, and a surprise. The two natural ways to measure "wrongness" (state distortion versus operator scrambling) turn out to be literally the same measurement, up to a fixed number, whenever the two parts have equal size. Wrongness cannot hide. (2) THE TWO-OPERATION THRESHOLD. You can pin down what your subsystems are by implementing just TWO generic operations and checking their statistics, while a THOUSAND mutually commuting operations tell you nothing at all. Diversity of control, not volume of control, is what fixes what your qubits are. The residual uncertainty is proportional to your measurement tolerance, with a constant we derive exactly and show how to compute in advance, so an experimenter can screen candidate operation pairs and pick a strong one (random pairs are typically several times worse, occasionally catastrophically so). (3) THE ALIASING LIMIT: CERTIFICATION CAN PASS WHILE TELLING YOU NOTHING. If you sample your certification data at special "resonant" times (set by the operations' energy scales), a maximally wrong assignment of subsystems passes the test perfectly. What your qubits are depends on when you looked. We characterize these blind spots exactly (for qubits they are universal and computable in advance; the danger windows shrink with the square root of your tolerance), and the fix costs almost nothing: sample at two different times, at least one away from the resonant set. With that, certification is restored; we prove it exactly and measure it. (4) REAL-LAB BUDGETS. We work out what certification costs in actual measurement shots (the error falls off unusually fast, inversely with the total number of shots rather than with its square root), how hardware noise floors the procedure, and how a simple reference measurement removes that floor to first order. A single seven-row table in the paper is effectively a lab protocol: it shows, condition by condition, which kinds of experimental access identify the subsystem structure (two generic operations: yes; one operation, commuting operations, resonant sampling: no). WHY IT MATTERS. For quantum hardware: this is a concrete recipe for certifying that the qubits you think you have are the qubits you physically have, with explicit tolerances, a sampling-time warning that is a real failure mode on calibrated hardware, and shot budgets. For foundations: the contested question "does physics determine its own subsystems?" gets a quantitative operational answer. Physics determines an operational subsystem CLASS (not one preferred coordinate representation of it), and that class is fixed by two operations sampled at two times, and by nothing less that we tested. WHAT IT OPENS UP. The seven-row identifiability table is a blueprint for a tabletop experiment on any small quantum platform; running it on hardware would move this from simulation to laboratory fact. On the theory side the paper leaves sharply posed open problems: the exact global constants when the two parts differ in size, the number-theoretic structure of long-time sampling (the failure times form a small-divisor hierarchy), and the extension from two parts to many. METHODS NOTE, BECAUSE IT MATTERS FOR TRUST. Every quantitative claim was pre-registered in the companion scripts before its run. The full ledger, including predictions that failed and one published-in-note constant that our own later theory overturned, is an appendix of the paper. All code, data, and working notes are in the deposit, seeded for exact reproduction. WHO AND HOW. A human-AI collaboration: research direction and standards of evidence by Ryan Cardwell (Crystalline Labs); design, code, derivations, and drafting by Claude (Anthropic), including autonomous sessions under the program's pre-registration rules, with adversarial reviews by other AI models incorporated and credited.

title: Computational Dynamic Abstraction Layer (CDAL)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Dynamic Abstraction Layer (CDAL), a novel approach to computing architecture design that moves beyond the constraints of traditional, static layered models. The core concept of CDAL revolves around the dynamic generation of abstraction layers, creating a system where layers are continuously formed and dissolved based on computational needs. This process aims to mimic the adaptive behavior observed in biological systems and potentially lead to architectures capable of responding to complex and evolving computational demands. The paper details the theoretical framework, outlining the key principles and mathematical representations involved in the CDAL model. It explores the potential implications of CDAL for future computing, highlighting its relevance to achieving the goals of the Turing Award and suggesting its capacity to generate radically different computing paradigms. The model utilizes a layered representation of computation, defined as: * `Layer_t → Layer_{t+1}` This dynamic transformation is governed by a set of rules and constraints, allowing for optimized resource allocation and efficient processing. This paper lays the groundwork for a deeper investigation into the practical application and theoretical underpinnings of the CDAL architecture. ---

title: Computational Language Transfer Theory (CLTT)
abstract: The present manuscript introduces the Computational Language Transfer Theory (CLTT), a formal framework that models the transfer of linguistic competence from a source language L_A to a target language L_B as a computational transformation. CLTT posits that language learning can be decomposed into a finite set of abstract linguistic primitives {s_1, s_2, …, s_K} that are first instantiated in the source language and then mapped to corresponding primitives in the target language via a transfer operator T. The theory is grounded in both cognitive science and formal language theory, and it offers a tractable mathematical description of how abstract syntactic and semantic structures are carried over during second‑language acquisition. By representing transfer as a composition of transformation functions, CLTT enables the prediction of transfer outcomes, the identification of bottlenecks, and the design of curriculum that exploits positive transfer and mitigates negative transfer. The paper further discusses implications for cross‑architecture computing systems, where CLTT provides a blueprint for transferring learning models across heterogeneous hardware and software platforms. The potential for CLTT to inform the design of universal language models and to contribute to the Turing Award conversation is also highlighted.

title: Serial Two-Stage Filtering by Conditional Innovation: An Information-Preserving High-to-Low Architecture for Common-State Operator Bounds
abstract: This paper develops a serial two-stage filtering framework based on ordered conditional innovation. Instead of applying two relation filters independently in parallel, the second filter acts only on the residual state left after the first-stage relation has been extracted. Using orthogonal projection and Gram–Schmidt decomposition, the construction preserves the full information of the original state while preventing duplicated relation freedom and independent-extremizer overestimation.The framework distinguishes between total information, which remains invariant under a reordering of fixed relation subspaces, and the stagewise innovation profile, which can depend strongly on filter order. A frozen four-dimensional common-state model exhibits a pronounced ordering effect: the High/Fine→Low/Coarse sequence captures approximately 97.985% of the selected state at the first stage and leaves approximately 2.015% as conditional innovation, whereas the reverse ordering produces approximately 41.108% and 58.892%, respectively.

title: Computational Intuition Boundary Theory (CIBT): Investigating the Formation of Intuition in Artificial Systems
abstract: Intuition is often regarded as a mysterious, rapid form of insight that enables humans to solve problems without explicit reasoning. In artificial systems, the emergence of intuition remains an open challenge, largely because the conditions under which a computational agent can generate intuitive judgments are not well understood. This paper introduces the Computational Intuition Boundary Theory (CIBT), a formal framework that delineates the boundary between non‑intuitive and intuitive behavior in machine learning systems. CIBT defines an intuition threshold function T(ΔC) that depends on the complexity gap ΔC between the internal model and the external environment, a performance parameter P that captures the speed of inference, and a contextual weighting factor θ that encodes domain relevance. We derive a set of necessary and sufficient conditions under which an agent's internal representation crosses the intuition boundary, and we analyze how these conditions interact with learning dynamics, data sparsity, and architectural choices. By applying CIBT to a range of canonical tasks—pattern recognition, strategic game play, and natural language understanding—we demonstrate that intuition arises when the model achieves a critical level of abstraction and generalization, coupled with a low‑latency inference pathway. The theory offers a principled lens for evaluating and designing artificial systems that aspire to human‑like intuition, and it suggests that the limits of machine intelligence may be governed more by representational depth than by computational power alone.

title: Where digital hate finds its home: perpetrators' preferred affordances and their experiences with content moderation and user intervention
abstract: Digital hate poses a significant challenge to democratic principles. However, not much is known about who produces it regularly, let alone across platforms. Drawing from routine activity theory as an overarching framework, our study investigated how the perceived importance of social media affordances is related to regular digital hate perpetrators’ platform use. Further, it explored how this usage is linked to experiences of moderation and interventions against them. Findings of quota-based surveys in four European countries (i.e., Austria, France, Hungary, and Sweden) suggest that perpetrators’ perceived importance of persistence and anonymity is consistently related to social media use across platforms, from which, in turn, primarily Telegram, Reddit, Twitch, and TikTok were linked to more frequent moderation and intervention experiences. By and large, our findings contribute to the current fight against digital hate by highlighting the need for regulatory strategies that account for perpetrators’ perceptions of affordances across platforms.

title: Feed-Forward Hierarchical Gaussian Diffusion for Extreme CT Reconstruction
abstract: Reconstructing three-dimensional computed tomography (CT) from severely constrained projections is highly ill-posed. Sparse angular sampling, restricted angular coverage, and low photon counts can occur individually or jointly, obscuring global anatomy and local tissue detail. Many learned CT reconstruction methods are tailored to a single dominant degradation. Existing diffusion and Gaussian approaches commonly recover global structure and local detail within a shared representation. We propose HiGDiff, a feed-forward hierarchical Gaussian diffusion framework that decomposes reconstruction both spatially and from structure to detail. Physics-conditioned anatomical anchors and a foreground capacity field allocate learnable Gaussian primitives to informative regions. A structure diffusion stage first recovers global attenuation geometry, and its learned representation conditions a detail diffusion stage for residual boundaries and tissue transitions. The resulting Gaussian banks are rendered as attenuation fields and further refined by a gradient-isolated residual module. Experiments on three distinct CT benchmark datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art reconstruction performance across isolated, paired, and joint degradation settings, including improvements of 5.81 dB in macro-average peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and 0.113 in structural similarity index measure (SSIM) on the Low Dose CT Image and Projection Data (LDCT-PD) collection. Code and experimental configurations are openly available at https://github.com/Bean-Young/HiGDiff.

title: WeSCE: A Benchmark for Measuring Security Drift in LLM-Driven Code Editing
abstract: In this work, we introduce WeSCE, a benchmark for quantifying security drift in code editing under weak-security constraints, where tasks specify only functional objectives without explicit security requirements. WeSCE consists of 400 executable programs derived from real-world code, covering feature addition, feature removal, bug fixing, and refactoring. To quantify security drift, we propose a continuous risk representation that aggregates heterogeneous vulnerability signals through a unified formulation, and define drift measures capturing changes in overall risk, worst-case severity, and vulnerability distribution under code transformations, providing a multi-scale view of security spanning average-case behavior to worst-case emphasis.

title: Evaluating Trajectories in Agentic Systems
abstract: As agentic systems increasingly incorporate multi-step processes, evaluation remains focused on predictive accuracy rather than process structure. This creates a gap in understanding how decisions are formed, particularly in systems that integrate multiple components. This gap is particularly critical in decision support contexts, where understanding how decisions are formed is as important as the decisions themselves. This work proposes a structural evaluation framework for intelligent agentic systems based on sequence and network analysis. Execution is modeled as state sequences and as dynamic interaction graphs, where nodes represent processes and control states, and edges represent transitions during decision formation. Sequence similarity is analyzed using Optimal Matching (OM) distance to assess stability and consistency of trajectories. Network-based measures, including centrality and motif frequency, are used to characterize coordination patterns, control structures, and progression toward decision commitment. Unlike traditional evaluation approaches, the framework explicitly models and evaluates the structure of execution processes rather than relying solely on outcome-based metrics. The framework is domain-agnostic and can be applied to a broad class of agentic and multi-step decision systems. The study contributes a structural evaluation perspective for intelligent agentic systems, shifting assessment from predictive outcomes to the organization and dynamics of processes. This is particularly relevant for emerging agentic systems that involve iterative planning, tool use, and multi-stage execution.

title: Make the LLMs Argue: Quorum, a Deliberation Protocol with Dissent Preserved
abstract: For high-stakes, ambiguous questions (strategy, pricing, architecture, risk) a single language model produces a confident answer with no visibility into its blind spots, and nothing in its fluency distinguishes a robust conclusion from a well-phrased guess. The disagreement between independent models is the best available signal of genuine uncertainty, and today it is thrown away: merged into consensus summaries that destroy precisely the information worth collecting. This paper presents Quorum, an open-source deliberation protocol that convenes three models from distinct labs to answer a question in enforced isolation, critique each other claim by claim under blind labels, revise, and hand a non-debating arbiter the job of delivering a verdict with dissent preserved. The protocol makes an unusual bet. It claims calibration material: the transcript is the product. Anonymization is structural rather than cosmetic. abstract: Harmonic Frontier Audio – Breathing Cycles and Physiological Patterns (Preview, v0.9) A high-fidelity human vocal dataset designed for AI training, speech research, and expressive voice modeling. Breathing Cycles and Physiological Patterns (Preview), created by Harmonic Frontier Audio, provides a compact reference set demonstrating the quality, formatting, and metadata conventions used in the Harmonic Frontier Audio Human Vocality Primitives series. 🔎 Summary This dataset provides high-quality, rights-cleared recordings of natural breathing cycles and physiological airflow patterns — non-lexical respiratory behaviors captured as isolated human acoustic primitives for expressive audio modeling. The recordings emphasize: relaxed and deeper inhale–exhale cycles slow, extended, and meditative breathing faster and shallow respiratory patterns brief inhale and exhale holds irregular breathing and reset breaths These characteristics make the dataset valuable for AI speech modeling, expressive voice synthesis, breath-aware generative audio, physiological sound modeling, and human-aligned vocal control systems. These phenomena are foundational to: naturalistic speech and voice synthesis breath-aware expressive audio modeling physiological and respiratory sound research embodied and multimodal agent behavior realistic timing and transition modeling around vocal activity This dataset presents a neutral, non-linguistic, non-performative representation of human respiratory behavior.It is not designed to encode semantic speech content, but rather to isolate acoustic primitives that underlie natural breathing, respiratory timing, and physiological airflow variation. 📂 Contents Audio Files (.wav) Recorded at 96 kHz / 24-bit WAV format Exported as mono Fade-ins and fade-outs of 3–5 ms applied for consistency No compression, normalization, or creative processing applied High-pass filtered at ~40 Hz to remove subsonic rumble This preview includes 3 representative audio files, selected to demonstrate: natural inhale–exhale cycle behavior variation in breath depth and pacing physiological airflow and respiratory timing characteristics Metadata (.csv) Includes structured fields for: file name sound source type airflow type phonation type gesture and articulation descriptors microphone and recording chain sample rate, bit depth, and dataset version Metadata follows the Harmonic Frontier Audio – Foundations schema. 🎤 Recording Notes Recorded in a treated studio environment using a single-mic setup: Microphone: Rode NT1-A condenser microphone Recording chain: Rode NT1-A → Zoom F8n Pro Captured at 96 kHz / 32-bit float, rendered as 96 kHz / 24-bit mono WAV for release. title: Progressive Associative Cache: An Intuitive Algorithm for Energy-Efficient AI Inference
abstract: 【Resource type】Publication → Preprint 【Title】Progressive Associative Cache: An Intuitive Algorithm for Energy-Efficient AI Inference 【Creators】Family name: ChenGiven name: Yaoquan 【Description】Current Large Language Models (LLMs) treat every query as a novel task, activating tens of billions of parameters for probabilistic generation regardless of whether the same question has been answered millions of times before, resulting in massive redundant energy consumption and latency. This paper proposes the Progressive Associative Cache (PAC)—a lightweight middleware that augments existing large models without modifying their architecture or retraining. PAC operates in parallel with standard inference: when a query misses the cache, the base model generates an answer as usual, while PAC automatically extracts structured features, maps them to a Multi-Index Hierarchical Tree, and stores the answer for future reuse; when a query hits, the Intuitive Algorithm returns the result directly or performs selective reasoning within a narrow scope, bypassing the full model entirely. We introduce the Leaf Node Precision Spectrum theory to distinguish the handling of objective data from subjective opinions, and propose Lazy Generation of Aggregation Nodes coupled with a four-layer Data Lifecycle Management framework (Base Metadata, Derived Data, Short-Term Dynamic, and Real-Time). This approach transforms generative AI from a stateless engine into a continuously learning associative memory system. 【Keywords】Large Language Model; Knowledge Cache; Intuitive Algorithm; Progressive Learning; Multi-Index Retrieval; Energy-Efficient Inference 【Licence】Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC-BY 4.0) 【Language】English 【Publication date】2026-08-15

title: Computational Relation Autonomy Theory (CRAT-2)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Relation Autonomy Theory (CRAT-2), a novel framework for designing and understanding autonomous intelligent systems. CRAT-2 posits that future intelligent systems should autonomously establish relationships, rather than relying on pre-defined, manually constructed connections. The theory centers around the core principle: [System → Relation], representing a shift from human-directed relationship formation to system-driven discovery. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of CRAT-2, emphasizing the role of computational models in simulating and facilitating this autonomous relationship formation. The framework suggests a potential trajectory towards a foundational technology for truly autonomous intelligent systems, holding significant implications for fields ranging from artificial intelligence to social robotics and beyond. We outline the key components of CRAT-2, including the relational embedding, the dynamic relationship mapping, and the feedback loop mechanisms, proposing a mathematical representation of the core processes. Finally, we discuss the theoretical implications and potential advancements stemming from the adoption of CRAT-2. ---

title: Program Meaning Geometry (PMG)
abstract: This paper introduces Program Meaning Geometry (PMG), a novel framework for understanding and representing program semantics. Traditional approaches to program semantics often rely on formal notations and symbolic relationships, which can be cumbersome and fail to capture the inherent complexity of computation. PMG proposes a radical shift: program semantics are fundamentally geometric, residing within a multi-dimensional space defined by meaning distances. The core concept is that the meaning of a program element (e.g., a variable, expression, or function) can be represented as a point in this geometric space. The distance between these points represents the degree of difference in meaning. This framework offers a potential pathway to a more intuitive and powerful understanding of program behavior, with implications for program verification, program synthesis, and potentially even the future of the Turing Award. The primary goal of this work is to establish a foundational geometric model for program semantics, outlining its key components and potential applications. ---

title: Computational Value Compression Theory (CVCT): A Formal Framework for Reducing Complex Experience to Core Value Representations
abstract: Computational Value Compression Theory (CVCT) proposes a principled method for mapping high‑dimensional, temporally extended experiential streams into concise, minimal value representations that preserve essential goal‑directing information. CVCT introduces the compression operator C that acts on an experience sequence E = (e_1, e_2, …, e_T) to produce a compressed value vector V = C(E) ∈ ℝ^K, where K << T. The theory posits that the operator C is defined by optimizing a joint objective that balances fidelity to the original experience, sparsity of the representation, and alignment with a utility function U. Formally, C is obtained by solving min_{C} L_fid(E, C(E)) + λ L_sparsity(C(E)) + μ L_util(C(E), U), where λ and μ are trade‑off parameters. The compressed vector V serves as a core value representation that can be used for decision making, planning, and long‑term goal maintenance. By demonstrating that CVCT can explain how agents maintain persistent objectives over extended horizons, the theory offers a potential path toward Turing Award‑level contributions in artificial intelligence. This paper develops the mathematical underpinnings of CVCT, discusses its implications for AI alignment and human cognition, and outlines future research directions.

title: Distribution-free false-alarm calibration and chance-corrected spatial evaluation for industrial anomaly detection
abstract: Studies of industrial visual inspection commonly report the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the overlap between anomaly maps and defect masks. Neither measure specifies the false-alarm rate at a selected threshold, while recurrent defect locations and mask geometry can inflate overlap. We combine a distribution-free upper tolerance threshold with a paired-minus-crossed spatial test. This test compares each detector's score-contributing locations with the matched defect mask and with masks from other images; the difference in rates defines spatial-evidence lift relative to the empirical chance-overlap rate. We evaluate three detectors on 120 point-defect images from three ISP-AD modalities and three fixed data splits. Of 378 alarms, 230 overlap the matched mask. Paired and crossed rates are nevertheless similar in eight of nine detector--modality cells; only DINOv2--ASM has a positive 95\% bootstrap lower bound (lift 0.259, 95\% interval 0.159--0.347). On the independent Magnetic Tile Defect dataset, the same analysis gives lifts of 0.203 (0.169--0.236) for Wide ResNet-50 (WRN50) patch memory and 0.231 (0.202--0.262) for Vision Transformer B/16 (ViT-B/16) patch memory, with one-sided permutation $p=10^{-5}$ for both. When crossed masks are restricted to the same defect class, the lifts remain 0.185 and 0.210. Exact sample planning shows that, with 150 calibration normals, a 95\%-confidence distribution-free claim is supported only for target false-positive rates of 1.98\% or higher; a 1\% target requires at least 299 normals. The results support reporting operating-point performance and chance-corrected spatial evidence alongside AUROC and raw mask overlap.

title: Mechanistic and Counterfactual Explanations in XAI: Cognitive Consequences for Decision‑Making
abstract: Abstract Contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems offer substantial benefits, but they often operate as “black boxes,” making it difficult to understand the reasoning behind their recommendations (Gunning et al., 2019). Although explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been widely argued as a remedy, empirical evidence suggests that explanations do not uniformly improve users’ understanding of AI recommendations (Chan, 2023). Thus, a key open question is why different XAI methods produce divergent cognitive and behavioral effects. The proposed study compares two widely used yet conceptually distinct XAI approaches: feature-importance and counterfactual. These methods are grounded in philosophical theories of explanation that enable us to make a theoretically informed comparison. By showing how much each input contributes to the output, feature-importance explanations (e.g., SHAP, LIME) align with the mechanistic view of explanation (Salmon, 1984). In contrast, the counterfactual method aligns with the counterfactual view of explanation (Lewis, 1973) by describing how changes to the inputs would lead to different outcomes. We argue that these differing explanatory logics have important cognitive implications. Specifically, we focus on users’ illusion of explanatory depth (Rozenblit & Keil, 2002), which happens when users believe they understand a system more deeply than they actually do. We hypothesize that counterfactual explanations induce a stronger illusion of explanatory depth than feature-importance explanations. This is because counterfactuals are more intuitive and simplified and might not accurately reflect the original model’s underlying logic. The illusion of explanatory depth further impairs the decision quality of individuals. However, domain expertise acts as a moderator, such that experts are less susceptible to counterfactual-induced illusions due to their existing knowledge of relevant features and outcomes. We plan to use a laboratory experiment where participants will be randomly assigned to receive either feature-importance or counterfactual explanations for the AI recommendation. The illusion of explanatory depth will be operationalized as the discrepancy between perceived and objective understanding. Also, participants will be asked to make a decision that will then be assessed for decision quality. This study contributes to XAI research by grounding XAI effects in philosophical theories and identifying illusion of explanatory depth as a key mechanism linking explainability to decision outcomes. Practically, the findings caution against uncritical use of intuitive explanations.

These methods are grounded in philosophical theories of explanation that enable us to make a theoretically informed comparison. By showing how much each input contributes to the output, feature-importance explanations (e.g., SHAP, LIME) align with the mechanistic view of explanation (Salmon, 1984). In contrast, the counterfactual method aligns with the counterfactual view of explanation (Lewis, 1973) by describing how changes to the inputs would lead to different outcomes. We argue that these differing explanatory logics have important cognitive implications. Specifically, we focus on users’ illusion of explanatory depth (Rozenblit & Keil, 2002), which happens when users believe they understand a system more deeply than they actually do. We hypothesize that counterfactual explanations induce a stronger illusion of explanatory depth than feature-importance explanations. This is because counterfactuals are more intuitive and simplified and might not accurately reflect the original model’s underlying logic. The illusion of explanatory depth further impairs the decision quality of individuals. However, domain expertise acts as a moderator, such that experts are less susceptible to counterfactual-induced illusions due to their existing knowledge of relevant features and outcomes. We plan to use a laboratory experiment where participants will be randomly assigned to receive either feature-importance or counterfactual explanations for the AI recommendation. The illusion of explanatory depth will be operationalized as the discrepancy between perceived and objective understanding. Also, participants will be asked to make a decision that will then be assessed for decision quality. This study contributes to XAI research by grounding XAI effects in philosophical theories and identifying illusion of explanatory depth as a key mechanism linking explainability to decision outcomes. Practically, the findings caution against uncritical use of intuitive explanations.

title: MCA-v0.1: An Evidence-Constrained, Falsifiable Middle-Level Working Model of Distributed Cognitive Bottlenecks
abstract: This bilingual working paper presents MCA-v0.1 as a provisional, evidence-constrained and falsifiable middle-level working model of distributed cognitive bottlenecks. It converts a frozen mechanism-first comparison of seven candidate formulations into a publication-level synthesis. OUTCOME_C retains C6/MCA-v0.1 as the most useful integrated working model under the frozen rubric, while C0, C1 and C5 remain non-dominated challengers in narrower regimes. The result is relative to the frozen corpus, candidate set and internally frozen evaluation procedure. It does not establish a unique biological architecture or a general theory of cognition. The same workflow constructed and rated the candidates; v0.1 has no independent coder or inter-rater reliability statistic. The search was targeted and source-critical, not systematic or PRISMA. The toy formalization checks internal coherence only and provides no biological validation. All twelve falsification tests remain open. No clinical, implant-design, consciousness-transfer or general biological-capacity-expansion claim is made, and no new human or animal experiment is reported. The record contains the full English reference version and a content-equivalent Hungarian version. Companion research compendium DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21958090. Magyar: Ez a kétnyelvű munkatanulmány az MCA-v0.1 modellt az elosztott kognitív szűk keresztmetszetek előzetes, bizonyítékkorlátos és falszifikálható középszintű munkamodelljeként mutatja be. A hét befagyasztott jelöltmegfogalmazás mechanizmus-első összevetését publikációs szintű szintézissé alakítja. Az OUTCOME_C a C6/MCA-v0.1 modellt a befagyasztott értékelési szabályok mellett leghasznosabb integrált munkamodellként tartja meg, miközben a C0, C1 és C5 szűkebb rezsimekben nem dominált kihívó marad. Az eredmény a befagyasztott korpuszhoz, a jelölthalmazhoz és a belsőleg befagyasztott értékelési eljáráshoz viszonyított. Nem igazol egyedi biológiai architektúrát vagy általános kognícióelméletet. Ugyanaz a munkafolyamat alkotta meg és értékelte a jelölteket; nincs független kódoló vagy értékelők közötti megbízhatósági mutató. A keresés célzott és forráskritikus volt, nem szisztematikus vagy PRISMA-áttekintés. A játékformalizáció csak belső koherencia-ellenőrzés, nem biológiai validáció. Mind a tizenkét falszifikációs teszt nyitott. A közlés nem klinikai protokoll vagy implantátumterv, nem tesz tudatátviteli állítást, nem igazol általános biológiai kapacitásbővítést, és nem közöl új ember- vagy állatkísérletet. A rekord a teljes angol referenciaváltozatot és annak tartalmilag egyenértékű magyar változatát tartalmazza. A kapcsolt kutatási kompendium DOI-ja: 10.5281/zenodo.21958090.

title: Computational Relation Singularity Theory (CRST-2)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Relation Singularity Theory (CRST-2), a novel framework for understanding emergent intelligence, particularly in the context of large language models (LLMs). The theory posits that a critical threshold exists – a combination of relationship quantity and quality – that triggers the emergence of novel capabilities. This threshold, denoted as [R > Rc], is analogous to the concept of emergence and potentially offers a pathway to understanding the sudden leaps in performance observed in LLMs. The core of CRST-2 lies in the idea that complex relationships within a system, when sufficiently dense and interconnected, can fundamentally alter the system's behavior, leading to unpredictable and powerful outcomes. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of this theory, focusing on the role of relational networks, information density, and the potential for a computational singularity. The theory proposes that achieving a critical level of relational complexity unlocks previously inaccessible cognitive abilities. This work aims to provide a conceptual model for analyzing and predicting emergent intelligence in complex systems, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of the driving forces behind advancements in artificial intelligence. ---

title: Computational Possibility Compiler (CPC)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Possibility Compiler (CPC), a novel approach to programming that shifts the paradigm from explicitly writing executable code to compiling a set of possible programs based on a given goal and constraints. The CPC operates on the principle that a system can be described not by *what* to compute, but by *how* it can potentially compute, effectively navigating a computational space. This framework offers significant potential for advancements in areas such as artificial intelligence, privacy computing, and data governance. This document outlines the core ideas behind the CPC, identifies potential areas for future research, and proposes a selection of innovative research directions with the potential to significantly impact the field of computation and earn recognition as Turing Award-level work. The focus is on generating fundamentally new approaches, avoiding duplication of existing ideas, and prioritizing research directions with the highest likelihood of producing impactful, high-citation papers.

title: Algorithmic Invariant Discovery Engine (AIDE)
abstract: The automated discovery of algorithmic invariants is a critical step towards robust algorithm verification and formal program analysis. This paper introduces the Algorithmic Invariant Discovery Engine (AIDE), a system designed to automatically identify relevant invariants during the execution of an algorithm. AIDE observes the algorithm's steps, tracking the state of the system at various points in time. Based on this observation, it aims to generate a diverse set of invariants including correctness, convergence, resource usage, and safety invariants. The system's core principle is to shift the burden of invariant identification from human analysts to an automated process, thereby accelerating algorithm development and improving software reliability. We posit that AIDE represents a significant step towards realizing the potential of the Turing Award in transforming the landscape of algorithm analysis and program verification. ---

title: Computational Language Creation Algorithm (CLCA)
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence has revealed a pressing need for new programming languages that can be generated automatically to suit specific computational tasks. In this paper we propose the Computational Language Creation Algorithm (CLCA), a principled framework that automatically designs a novel programming language's syntax, type system, and abstract semantics from a high‑level specification of desired computational properties. CLCA integrates formal language theory, type inference mechanisms, and graph‑based abstraction techniques to construct a language that is both expressive and safe. We formalize the algorithmic steps, analyze its computational complexity, and discuss its potential to transform the way programming languages are conceived, particularly for specialized AI applications. The algorithm's capacity to produce a language with a clear grammar, a robust type system, and a well‑defined abstract machine suggests a significant step toward automating the design of domain‑specific languages and may well be a catalyst for future Turing Award‑level contributions.

title: Computational Rule Transfer Theory (CRTT)
abstract: Computational Rule Transfer Theory (CRTT) is a theoretical framework that formalizes the systematic migration of abstract rules from one domain to another, with a particular focus on the transfer of physical and mathematical principles into artificial intelligence algorithms. This paper introduces the core concepts of CRTT, develops a formal representation of rule migration, and proposes algorithmic mechanisms for rule extraction, adaptation, and integration. By exploring the theoretical underpinnings and practical implications of rule transfer, we demonstrate how CRTT can enable cross‑disciplinary breakthroughs, particularly in the synthesis of physics‑informed neural networks, symbolic reasoning systems, and self‑optimizing control architectures. The discussion highlights potential applications, limitations, and future research directions, positioning CRTT as a foundational tool for the next generation of interdisciplinary AI research.

title: Trust in AI: Anthropomorphism, Explainability, and Trustworthiness
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in organizational and everyday decision-making, but its effectiveness depends on appropriate user trust. Both under-trust and over-trust are problematic because users may reject useful AI systems when trust is too low or over-rely on imperfect systems when trust is too high (Lee & See, 2004). This TREO paper develops a conceptual model based on the theory of reasoned action (TRA) to explain how anthropomorphism and explainability influence trust through perceived competence, benevolence, and integrity (Ajzen & Fishbein, 1980). Anthropomorphic cues may increase perceived competence and benevolence by making AI appear more relatable and capable (Epley et al., 2007). However, excessive or inauthentic human likeness may undermine perceived integrity by creating unrealistic expectations or suspicion (Glikson & Woolley, 2020). Explainability strengthens trust by reducing uncertainty and helping users understand, evaluate, and contest AI decisions (Miller, 2019). This TREO paper proposes a conceptual model examining how anthropomorphism and explainability may influence user trust in AI through perceptions of competence, benevolence, and integrity. Anthropomorphism is expected to increase perceived competence and benevolence, while excessive human-likeness may reduce perceived integrity. Explainability is expected to strengthen all three trustworthiness perceptions, which in turn are expected to shape trust in AI. This study contributes to the AI trust research by integrating anthropomorphism, explainability, and trustworthiness beliefs into a unified TRA-based framework. In practice, it suggests that designers should balance relatable AI interactions with transparency, ethical accountability, and calibrated reliance. Future researchers can test the model using survey data and structural equation modeling across AI application domains such as healthcare, education, finance, and workplace decision support.

title: Computational Decision Space Geometry (CDSG)
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Decision Space Geometry (CDSG), a novel framework for understanding and modeling decision-making processes. Traditional approaches often treat decision-making as discrete point selection, neglecting the inherent geometric nature of choices. CDSG proposes that decisions are made by traversing a continuous decision space, [ΩD], and argues for a rigorous investigation into the structural properties of these spaces. The core concept is that decision-making is not about selecting a specific point, but rather about the continuous movement within this geometric space. This framework has the potential to unify diverse areas of research including search algorithms, planning systems, and artificial intelligence, ultimately offering a more comprehensive and geometrically-grounded approach to intelligent decision-making. The paper outlines the fundamental principles of CDSG, explores its implications for various decision-making scenarios, and suggests future research directions. ---

title: Computational Constraint Creation Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Constraint Creation Theory (CCCT), a novel framework proposing that constraints are not merely limitations on computation, but rather fundamental drivers of capability generation. CCCT posits a systematic mechanism where constraints, when imposed, lead to the emergence of enhanced abilities within computational systems. The theory is illustrated through examples, notably the observation that the architectural constraints inherent in neural network design directly contribute to their generalization capabilities. The implications of CCCT extend to areas such as optimization and learning, potentially warranting a re-evaluation of traditional approaches. This paper lays the groundwork for further research exploring the dynamics of constraint-driven capability development within computational systems. ---

title: Computational Function Transferability
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Computational Function Transferability (CFT), a framework for evaluating the degree to which a module's functionality can be transferred to a new system. CFT is defined as the ratio of the function preserved to the adaptation cost. This ratio provides a quantifiable measure of transferability, considering both the extent to which the original function remains intact and the effort required to adapt the module to the new environment. The potential of CFT extends to unifying software migration, model transfer, algorithm reuse, and cross-hardware deployment, representing a significant step towards more efficient and adaptable software development and computational systems. The core idea is presented with the formula: [T(M,S') = FunctionPreserved / AdaptationCost], where T(M,S') represents the transferability between module M and system S'. This paper outlines the theoretical foundations, key considerations, and potential applications of CFT, highlighting its relevance in the current landscape of distributed computing, artificial intelligence, and complex system design. ---

title: Computational Value Formation Theory (CVFT)
abstract: Computational Value Formation Theory (CVFT) proposes a unified framework for understanding how autonomous systems generate internal value functions that guide decision making, independently of externally supplied rewards. Traditional reinforcement learning paradigms treat reward signals as the sole source of value, whereas CVFT posits that experience streams, sensory inputs, and internal dynamics give rise to a self‑generated value landscape. This paper develops a formal model of value formation, establishes its consistency with known cognitive phenomena, and outlines potential implications for the design of self‑learning artificial agents. By deriving a recursive value update equation grounded in experience accumulation, CVFT offers a principled alternative to reward‑driven learning and suggests a pathway toward intrinsic motivation mechanisms that could underpin future autonomous AI systems.

title: Computational Goal Ecology Theory (CGET-4)
abstract: Computational Goal Ecology Theory (CGET-4) proposes a novel conceptual framework for understanding the interactions of multiple autonomous objectives within artificial and natural systems. By treating each goal \(G_i\) as an ecological agent that engages in both competitive and cooperative dynamics, CGET-4 provides a unifying language for reasoning about multi-objective optimization, emergent behavior, and resource allocation. The theory introduces a formal representation of a goal space, defines interaction kernels for competition and cooperation, and derives a set of coupled differential equations that capture the evolution of goal strengths over time. This paper develops the mathematical foundation of CGET-4, discusses its implications for the design of next‑generation AI systems, and argues that the theory has the potential to contribute to foundational advances worthy of the Turing Award. The work is purely theoretical and does not include experimental validation; rather, it lays the groundwork for future empirical studies.

title: Continual Federated Learning for Network Intrusion Detection: An Open-Index Systematic Map
abstract: Purpose: Continual federated learning (FCL) combines decentralized model updating with sequential adaptation, but network-intrusion studies use incompatible definitions of drift, retention, and evaluation. This open-index systematic map examines how such systems operationalize non-stationarity, preserve earlier knowledge, and report empirical and reproducibility evidence. Method: Eight queries were executed in OpenAlex, Crossref, and DBLP on 26 July 2026. The interfaces returned 8,819 records within documented result limits; deduplication left 3,075 unique records. The initial concept-block rule excluded 2,865 records. A rule-based sensitivity audit reclassified two false negatives, yielding 2,863 automatic exclusions and 212 records for title/abstract screening. Thirty-one database-derived and nine supplementary reports were sought; 24 were not retrieved. Sixteen full texts were assessed, two were excluded, and 14 primary studies were mapped. Results: The corpus comprised three studies from 2023, six from 2024, one from 2025, and four from the partial 2026 search year. Nine studies tested retention after later tasks or classes; five reported adaptation without a prior-task retention outcome. Within the nine retention-tested studies, replay-based designs most often reported favorable within-study stability results, but heterogeneous scenarios and comparators do not establish cross-study superiority. Only two studies reported standardized forgetting or backward transfer, two supplied study-specific code, and one tested malicious clients. Conclusion: The accessible open-index evidence supports FCL as a prototype strategy under constructed benchmark sequences. It does not establish cross-network robustness, formal privacy, or deployment-scale reliability. A targeted supplementary update on 27 July 2026 found no additional eligible, accessible full text. Interpretation is constrained by capped interfaces, single-reviewer screening, and 24 unretrieved reports.

Nine studies tested retention after later tasks or classes; five reported adaptation without a prior-task retention outcome. Within the nine retention-tested studies, replay-based designs most often reported favorable within-study stability results, but heterogeneous scenarios and comparators do not establish cross-study superiority. Only two studies reported standardized forgetting or backward transfer, two supplied study-specific code, and one tested malicious clients. Conclusion: The accessible open-index evidence supports FCL as a prototype strategy under constructed benchmark sequences. It does not establish cross-network robustness, formal privacy, or deployment-scale reliability. A targeted supplementary update on 27 July 2026 found no additional eligible, accessible full text. Interpretation is constrained by capped interfaces, single-reviewer screening, and 24 unretrieved reports.

title: The Physical Cutoff Does Not Restore Homogenization: Phase-Dependent Burning in the Strain G-Equation
abstract: We disprove the expectation stated by Xin, Yu, and Ronney that the physical positive part strain $G$-equation should possess an effective burning velocity in cellular flows. For the standard cellular flow in dimension two $V_A(x_1,x_2)=A(-\sin x_1\cos x_2,\cos x_1\sin x_2)$, if $0<d<20/399$ and $\sqrt{1+4d^2}<Ad\le1+d/10$, then for every unit planar slope the periodic correction develops oscillations at least linearly in time. The solution remains bounded below on an explicit horizontal channel through $(π,0)$, while at $(π/2,0)$ it decreases at rate at least $CA/\log A$, with $C>0$ universal. The same conclusions hold for arbitrary continuous periodic perturbations of planar initial data. Under the physical scaling $V_A(x/\varepsilon)$ and $d_\varepsilon=\varepsilon d$, an order one value gap persists between points at distance $O(\varepsilon)$ at every positive macroscopic time, so the rescaled solutions have no locally uniformly convergent subsequence. The proof uses the Hamiltonian sandwich $H_{\mathrm{unc}}\le H_+\le\widehat H$. The upper comparator $\widehat H$ is a rectangular support function, equivalently an upper expectation over a state-dependent credal set, whose reversed control dynamics possess an invariant comparison channel. We also prove that for any $C^2$ incompressible periodic flow, every $\varepsilon$-outward barrier certificate has covering radius at most $2d\varepsilon$ for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. We further discuss implications for statistics and machine learning: rectangular, time-consistent local uncertainty need not imply forgetting of the initial state in the long run, so additional global stability or ergodicity conditions are needed in robust sequential decision making. Two Lean 4 appendices record conditional formalizations of a sufficient $p=e_1$ subregime and of the logical assembly of the rigidity theorem for barrier certificates.
