title: Academic Experience Platforms: AI Meets Cognitive Science
abstract: The growing demand for online and hybrid education has revealed several opportunities for improvement in contemporary educational ecosystems and infrastructure. Traditional Learning Management Systems (LMS) function as content databases with limited personalization capabilities, while corporate Learning Experience Platforms (LXP) emphasize skill acquisition without supporting comprehensive academic activities. The current work proposes the Academic Experience Platform (AXP), an AI-powered system to address knowledge fragmentation, algorithmic transparency, and academic rigor through evidence-based instructional design grounded in established instructional theories. The AXP framework is supported by Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) to address the following critical needs: (1) preventing cognitive overload through intelligent content design which lowers mental overstimulation (extraneous load) while maximizing productive learning efforts (germane load), (2) applying diagnostic assessments that adapt content based on learners' existing knowledge to avoid the expertise reversal effect in which advanced learners waste time on material they've already mastered, and (3) leveraging learning analytics to create personalized pathways while maintaining transparency and learner agency. Unlike existing platforms, the AXP aims to offer pedagogical ecosystems for both instructors and learners. The AXP shall enable instructors in designing evidence-based microlearning modules, implementing diagnostic assessments, and accessing analytics that enhances instructional design. Learners get on-demand access to role-based content, custom organic recommendations, and structured progressions from lower-order to higher-order thinking skills aligned with Bloom's Taxonomy. The framework integrates competency-based education principles with mechanisms to prevent knowledge fragmentation. Learning analytics track concept coverage, identify gaps in knowledge networks, and prompt integration activities, while checkpoint assessments ensure learners progress from isolated skill acquisition to integrated competency. This research contributes theoretical foundations for AXP development and practical design guidelines for educational technology developers, institutional decision-makers, and instructional designers seeking to transform academic delivery models while maintaining rigor and supporting workforce readiness.

title: Analisis Sentimen Pemilu Amerika Serikat Menggunakan Metode Combine Convolational Neural Network (CNN) Dan Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)
abstract: Media sosial seperti X (sebelumnya Twitter) telah menjadi platform utama masyarakat dalam menyampaikan pandangan politik secara real-time, namun analisis sentimen pada data media sosial menghadapi tantangan berupa kompleksitas bahasa dan volume data yang besar. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis sentimen opini publik terhadap Pemilu Amerika Serikat 2024 menggunakan metode hybrid Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) dan Recurrent Neural Network (RNN). Penelitian ini mengusulkan pendekatan hybrid CNN-RNN yang menggabungkan keunggulan CNN dalam ekstraksi fitur lokal dan RNN dalam pemahaman konteks sekuensial untuk meningkatkan akurasi klasifikasi sentiment Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa model Hybrid CNN-RNN memberikan performa terbaik dengan akurasi 69,53%, precision 70,12%, recall 69,53%, dan F1-Score 66,33%, mengungguli model CNN (akurasi 66,95%, F1-Score 67,30%) dan model RNN (akurasi 51,93%, F1-Score 41,83%). Temuan penelitian mengungkapkan bahwa kombinasi CNN dan RNN dalam model hybrid efektif menggabungkan keunggulan kedua metode, menghasilkan representasi data yang lebih lengkap sehingga meningkatkan kemampuan klasifikasi sentimen. Penelitian ini berkontribusi bagi pengamat politik, analis data, dan lembaga riset untuk memantau dan menganalisis sentimen publik, membantu dalam memprediksi hasil pemilu, dan merencanakan strategi kampanye yang lebih efektif.

title: Part VII Revelation Is Not Formation: From Hidden-State Prediction to Open Temporal Processes
abstract: Probabilistic prediction is frequently described using metaphors of discovery: a model is said to "see" the future, uncover a hidden state, or reveal an event that already exists beyond the present. Such language is useful in some mathematical settings but becomes misleading when transferred to temporally open, interactive systems. This paper develops a formal distinction between state revelation and state formation. In a random graph model such as Erdős–Rényi G(n,p), a realized graph can be treated as a hidden object whose properties are progressively revealed through a filtration. Conditional expectations generate a Doob martingale describing the evolution of knowledge about an already realized object. The mathematical object itself, however, is not transformed by the observer's successive revelations. This structure differs fundamentally from an open interactive process in which future states are generated through ongoing interactions among the system, its environment, and the actions taken within it. In such systems, forecasts may themselves become causal inputs. A prediction can therefore modify the decision process that contributes to the subsequent state. The resulting problem cannot be represented adequately as the progressive revelation of a pre-existing hidden future state. The distinction has important implications for artificial intelligence forecasting. An AI system may infer future-oriented information from present indicators with extraordinary accuracy without thereby observing the future, accessing a future state, or establishing that such a state exists independently of the process through which it will be formed. The paper argues that the central conceptual error is not probabilistic uncertainty itself, but the conflation of the evolution of information about a system with the evolution of the system being modeled. The argument is deliberately independent of any particular metaphysical theory of time: even granting, for the sake of argument, that the future is determined in some sense, an agent's location in the present does not thereby become a location from which the future is observed. The paper concludes by proposing a distinction between two classes of temporal modeling: revelatory models, which infer properties of a state treated as already determined, and formative models, which represent systems whose future states emerge through continuing interaction. The fundamental limit of forecasting in an open temporal system is not necessarily predictive uncertainty, but the fact that the state being predicted may be partly constituted by the ongoing interaction through which the prediction itself enters the system. Central thesis: "Revelation Is Not Formation. The evolution of knowledge about a system is not the evolution of the system itself." "The fundamental limit of forecasting in an open temporal system is not necessarily predictive uncertainty, but the fact that the state being predicted may be partly constituted by the ongoing interaction through which the prediction itself enters the system."

title: Computational Capability Phase Diagram (CCPD)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Capability Phase Diagram (CCPD), a novel theoretical framework inspired by traditional phase diagrams in thermodynamics and materials science. The core idea of the CCPD is to map the landscape of computational systems – defined by a set of parameters – into a phase space where different regions correspond to distinct computational capabilities. These capabilities aren't simply quantified by metrics like FLOPS or memory size, but rather encompass emergent properties like problem-solving efficiency, adaptability, and the ability to perform complex reasoning. The CCPD posits that, analogous to physical phases, computational systems can exist in different states of organization and potential, dictated by the interplay of these parameters. The diagram aims to provide a predictive tool, potentially allowing us to anticipate and understand the emergence of intelligent behaviors in increasingly complex computational systems. This work lays the groundwork for exploring the potential of the CCPD to guide the design and development of future AI architectures. ---

title: Computational Event Grammar
abstract: This paper introduces Computational Event Grammar (CEG), a novel approach to program representation that moves beyond traditional instruction-based paradigms. CEG posits that programs are fundamentally composed of events linked by relations, rather than discrete instructions. The core concept is that a program is defined as an event plus its associated relations, represented as [E_1 ∘ E_2]. This grammar aims to capture the inherent sequential and conditional nature of computation more naturally, potentially offering a foundation for future programming languages and a viable candidate for consideration in the Turing Award. The paper outlines the key principles of CEG, explores its potential benefits, and discusses its relationship to existing programming paradigms. We present a formal definition of CEG, including the rules for combining events and relations, and highlight its advantages in representing complex computational processes.

title: Computational Task Energy Landscape (CTEL)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Task Energy Landscape (CTEL) framework, a novel approach to optimization and search problems. The core concept revolves around representing the search space as an energy landscape, where solutions are viewed as points within this landscape. This landscape is characterized by distinct regions representing varying costs, including high-cost areas, low-cost areas, and local optima. The algorithm iteratively navigates this landscape, seeking the lowest-cost path from an initial state to an optimal solution. We explore the potential of CTEL to unify optimization, search algorithms, and computational complexity analysis, highlighting its theoretical implications and potential for realizing a Turing Award-worthy contribution. This document outlines the fundamental principles, formalization, and potential of the CTEL framework. ---

title: Computational Rule Singularity Theory (CRS)
abstract: The field of artificial intelligence has long sought mechanisms by which an autonomous system can surpass human ingenuity. This paper introduces Computational Rule Singularity Theory (CRS), a formal framework that describes how a system can generate, refine, and recursively apply rules to achieve performance exceeding human capabilities. CRS is built on the premise that a system capable of discovering better rules than those devised by human experts can enter a phase of rule‑recursive enhancement, leading to exponential growth in problem‑solving power. We articulate the theoretical foundations of CRS, outline the computational mechanisms for rule creation and refinement, and examine the conditions under which recursive rule enhancement may converge toward a singularity in which superintelligence emerges. The potential for CRS to inform future AI architectures and its implications for the Turing Award are discussed.

title: AI for Healthcare: How Can Hospitals Share Data to Build Better Models?
abstract: The study has explored the importance of sharing data in hospitals for training Artificial Intelligence (AI) models. It has been observed that sharing data in the model training faces challenges such as ethical and privacy concerns, and the revelation of sensitive data of the patients. AI has been used in the detection of skin diseases and in the prediction of cancer from X-Ray images. However, limited data within a single hospital poses challenges and raises data privacy concerns. Investigation on this topic was found to be effective for improving the patient survival and recovery rates. This includes Federated Learning techniques, Homomorphic encryption, synthetic data generation and differential privacy.

title: Physics-informed VAE-EVT for Tail Aware Radio Map Prediction
abstract: Ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC) requires precise identification of spatial regions where the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) falls below an outage threshold. In this context, an outage refers to instances in which SNR falls below a specified threshold, which, for URLLC, can be as stringent as the 0.1% quantile of the SNR distribution. Traditional generative radio map models tend to focus on reconstructing average signal levels, often overlooking the low SNR that is crucial for accurate outage prediction. To address this limitation, we introduce a physics- and tail-informed VAE-EVT (variational autoencoder-extreme value theory) framework that distinctly models both the bulk and tail distribution of SNR. Our approach begins with a physics-informed preprocessing stage that extracts deterministic features, including line-of-sight, shadowing, and distance, from the scene geometry. A dual-latent encoder then captures the bulk SNR using a Gaussian mixture and the tail using a generalized Pareto distribution (GPD). By employing a modified variational objective, the model is trained to jointly supervise both regimes, ensuring focused attention on extreme fading events. Evaluated on the RadioMapSeer dataset, our method achieves an SNR RMSE of 4.83 dB in the outage region defined by the low threshold of 0.1% SNR quantile. This significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art GAN-based model, which records an SNR RMSE of 21.90 dB, with the performance gap widening as the outage threshold becomes more stringent.

title: Judgy AI: I Trust It If It Tells Me What I Want to Hear
abstract: There has been a proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) systems that provide classifications of people (i.e., feedback) based on personal attributes such as personality, looks, and qualifications (Ryan-Mosley, 2021). We refer to AI applications that provide feedback on personal attributes as judgy AI. A commercial application of such systems, used by cosmetic companies, is to assess for skin conditions such as redness, pores, and wrinkles and use the feedback to suggest purchases (Eriksson & Kenalemang, 2023). Many of these systems use AI to assess images people upload, classifying their appearance based on models trained on images of others. The AI literature has examined how people react to algorithms, and in doing so, has found that people can be both averse to and appreciative of them (Logg et al., 2019; Turel & Kalhan, 2023), which suggests that context (e.g., how the AI is used) may play a role in people’s feelings toward them. Our interest, in this study, is in examining how people react to personal judgments from an algorithm, and specifically, whether those reactions influence their purchase intentions. Such findings are useful in understanding not only user reactions to algorithmic feedback but also how such feedback may drive consumption. Drawing on expectation-confirmation theory, we tested a model exploring how confirmatory feedback drives perceptions of usefulness of the algorithm, and how both directly, and indirectly through satisfaction and trust of the algorithm, these perceptions influence purchase intentions. Participants used a classification algorithm that provided feedback on their appearance, and our preliminary findings illustrate how such algorithmic feedback may ultimately influence purchasing behaviors. This study contributes to the AI literature by examining how people react to judgmental feedback from AI systems and how these reactions may influence their consumption behaviors. For practice, findings from this study speak to the effectiveness of using such systems as sales tools.

title: Computational Value Explanation Theory (CVET)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Value Explanation Theory (CVET), a formal framework that bridges the gap between decision-making processes and the values they produce. By positing a mapping from decisions to values (Decision → Value), CVET offers a principled way to generate explanations for why particular outcomes or actions are deemed important. The theory is grounded in causal reasoning and information theory, and it integrates seamlessly with existing explainable AI techniques. We present a rigorous mathematical formulation of the CVET axioms, illustrate the theory with illustrative examples drawn from machine learning and economics, and discuss its implications for the interpretability of artificial intelligence systems. CVET is positioned as a potential catalyst for the next generation of explainable AI methods, enabling systems to articulate not only *what* decisions they make but also *why* those decisions carry value.

title: Computational Rule Stability Theory (CRST-2)
abstract: Computational Rule Stability Theory (CRST-2) introduces a formal framework for understanding why certain algorithmic rules remain valid over extended periods of time. By treating each algorithmic rule as a dynamical entity R_t evolving over discrete time steps t, CRST-2 posits that a rule is stable if it satisfies the approximate equality R_t ≈ R_{t+n} for all sufficiently large t and for some fixed n. This paper develops the core ideas behind CRST-2, derives necessary and sufficient conditions for stability, and discusses its implications for algorithm longevity and the broader field of theoretical computer science. The theory offers a potential explanation for the enduring success of classical algorithms and provides a foundation for designing future algorithms with guaranteed long‑term performance.

title: Computational Reality Model Transfer Theory (CRMTR): A New Paradigm for Domain Generalization
abstract: The ability to transfer knowledge learned in one context to another is a fundamental challenge in artificial intelligence and cognitive science. Existing approaches to domain adaptation often rely on statistical alignment or supervised fine‑tuning, which can be brittle when the target domain exhibits substantial distributional shifts. This paper introduces Computational Reality Model Transfer Theory (CRMTR), a conceptual framework that formalizes the transfer of a world model constructed in one domain (M_A) to a different domain (M_B). By treating a domain as a structured reality consisting of perceptual inputs, internal representations, and generative dynamics, CRMTR articulates a set of transformation principles that preserve the semantic integrity of the model while allowing it to adapt to new environmental constraints. The theory leverages a hierarchical decomposition of reality into observable, latent, and causal layers, and proposes an algorithmic pathway for reconstructing the target model via inference over a shared latent space. Potential applications span robotics, autonomous navigation, and cross‑modal learning, and the framework offers a principled route toward solving the long‑standing generalization problem in machine learning.

title: ROMEO-HYDRA v0.2.0 — Information Folding Topology (Structure-Before-Specificity)
abstract: Release that elevates information folding as a base principle of computer topology inside ROMEO-HYDRA. Principle: any digital object induces a space. Stable information lives in structural invariants (components, identity cycles, critical order). High-entropy detail is scaffold and can be discarded or regenerated under a rate budget. Encoding invariants is folding; reconstruction is unfolding. Metaphor: the cell packs ~2 m of DNA into a nucleus smaller than 0.5 mm — not by deleting sequence, but by hierarchical folding that preserves function. The same idea applied to files, documents, ledgers and media: keep what must persist, fold away what does not. Includes: - romeo.topology.fold (fold_bytes, fold_text, fold_file) - romeo.tools.video (YC-ready offline compress as a media instance of the same principle) - docs/TOPOLOGY.md - Offline / Termux aarch64 compatible APIs - Continuity with prior DOIs (concept 10.5281/zenodo.21744014) Author: Luis Angel Vazquez Martinez. License: AGPL-3.0-or-later (evaluation) / commercial EMMOROR on request.

title: HybridDetect: Detecting Partial AI Contamination in Student Essays via Multi-Class Classification (code and trained models)
abstract: Code, trained models, and evaluation artifacts accompanying the FedCSIS 2026 paper "HybridDetect: Detecting Partial AI Contamination in Student Essays via Multi-Class Classification" (Dan & Nakayama, Proc. 21st Conference on Computer Science and Intelligence Systems, pp. 495-500, 2026). HybridDetect reframes AI-text detection as a seven-class contamination-level problem (0%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 90%, 100% AI content) rather than a binary human/AI decision. It combines a fine-tuned RoBERTa-base model with an XGBoost classifier over 36 handcrafted linguistic features via weighted soft voting, reaching 79.9% accuracy / 0.798 macro F1 on the 7-class task and 0.876 binary F1 (n = 7,501 test essays). Contents: hybriddetect-code-v1.0.zip - full pipeline (dataset generation, training, evaluation, figures, statistics verification) plus saved metrics and predictions; hybriddetect-roberta-v1.0.zip - fine-tuned RoBERTa weights, config, tokenizer; hybriddetect-xgboost-v1.0.zip - XGBoost model, feature scaler, feature names. The source corpus (AI vs Human Text, Kaggle) is third-party data and is not redistributed; the pipeline regenerates the 50,001 hybrid essays from it deterministically (fixed seed 42). Development repository: https://github.com/DanielDanLab/HybridDetect

title: A Digital Decision-Support Framework for Green Hydrogen-Based Steam Production in the Food Industry
abstract: The decarbonization of industrial steam production, representing up to 57% of energy use in the food industry, is critical for achieving EU climate neutrality goals. This study developed an integrated digital framework for the research project Hy4GreenSteam to optimize green-hydrogen integration through advanced predictive modeling. The employed LightGBM gradient-boosting algorithms were trained on 68,697 PV power measurements and 57,000 meteorological observations from 2020 to 2022. A “Production-Split” methodology was introduced for 24 h ahead forecasting, segmenting training into high (>2 kW) and low (≤2 kW) production regimes to manage solar heteroscedasticity. Results show the 15 min model achieved an R2 of 0.868 and the 1 h model an R2 of 0.832, while the day-ahead model—trained exclusively on information available at forecast issue time—achieved an R2 of 0.701, a 70% relative improvement over same-time-yesterday persistence. A complementary regime analysis shows that the production regime is predictable with 90.7% accuracy and quantifies the accuracy headroom of regime-specialized models (oracle R2 0.794). These methods were integrated into a real-time React-based platform that calculates optimal H2/CH4 blending; for the reference pilot configuration, driven by measured on-site PV generation, the computed CO2 emission reduction reaches 34% relative to natural-gas-only operation during high-solar operating intervals. Predictive modeling combined with a Digital Twin interface provides a TRL 6 decision-support solution, demonstrated in a relevant industrial environment, for managing renewable sources in industrial hydrogen applications.

title: Shape Operator PCA: Curvature-Aware Projections for Geometric Machine Learning
abstract: In this paper, we propose SHOPCA (Shape Operator-based Principal Component Analysis), a novel method for unsupervised metric learning and dimensionality reduction that incorporates differential geometric information into the covariance structure of classical PCA. SHOPCA regularizes the global covariance matrix using the mean shape operator, defined as the average of the absolute local shape operators estimated from the data manifold, steering principal components toward directions of both maximum variance and informative curvature. A single trace-normalized mixing coefficient $α$ controls the regularization, recovering standard PCA at $α= 0$ and a curvature-driven embedding as $α\to \infty$. We further introduce a fully unsupervised criterion for selecting $α$ based on the spectral eigengap of the regularized covariance matrix, maximizing the relative separation between the top-$d$ and remaining eigenvalues without using class labels. We evaluate SHOPCA on more than 50 real-world benchmark datasets, comparing it with PCA, ISOMAP, and UMAP using Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), Normalized Mutual Information (NMI), Fowlkes-Mallows index (FM), and V-measure. Results show that SHOPCA consistently improves clustering quality over PCA across a broad range of datasets and surpasses UMAP on small-sample settings, where iterative neighborhood-based manifold estimation can degrade. SHOPCA is computationally tractable, parameter-efficient, and applicable to domains requiring fully unsupervised, geometry-aware dimensionality reduction.

title: LongDocBench: Benchmarking TOC Hierarchy and Contextual Relationship Recovery in Long Documents
abstract: Parsing visual documents into machine-readable representations is fundamental to document intelligence. Existing benchmarks focus on page-level element recognition, reading order, formula recognition, and table structure. Long documents, however, also require document-level structure recovery. This includes reconstructing cross-page table-of-contents (TOC) hierarchies and identifying typed links from tables and figures to their captions, notes, and sources, often in one-to-many form. Because these structures are covered only partially or subsumed within broader parsing protocols, existing benchmarks cannot directly evaluate two key document-level tasks: \emph{Table-of-Contents Hierarchy Recovery} and \emph{Contextual Relationship Recovery}. To benchmark these two tasks, we introduce \textsc{LongDocBench}, comprising 85 real-world financial reports, textbooks, and academic papers spanning 2,582 pages, with up to 105 pages per document. It provides human-verified annotations for 3,937 heading nodes (mean node depth 3.55; maximum depth 9) and 3,258 contextual relationships annotated across 2,680 table and figure objects. We further evaluate both the downstream utility and recoverability of these structures. Long-document question-answering experiments show that human-verified TOC hierarchies and contextual relationships improve reasoning, with their combination providing complementary benefits. Meanwhile, representative document parsers remain limited on both recovery tasks despite strong page-level performance. To support further progress, we publicly release \textsc{LongDocBench} and its evaluation protocol and reproducible testbed for advancing document-level structure recovery in long documents.

title: The Instruction Tax on Factual Recall: Base Models Can Beat Their Instruction-Tuned Counterparts
abstract: We present our solution to the AKBC LM-KBC 2026 Shared Task, where we achieved a score of 0.6836 on the official leaderboard, more than double the baseline of 0.2964. This task requires generating all possible objects for subject-relation pairs using a language model with up to 32 billion parameters, with no retrieval or fine-tuning involved. We show that the prompting methodology is as important as the model architecture: while the instructiontuned model version achieves 0.5681 with its chat interface, the base model achieves 0.6836 when prompted using text completion. Thus, instruction tuning decreases factual recall; we refer to this effect as the instruction tax, which is caused by the model's weights rather than the prompting method.Our final solution is fairly straightforward: we prompt the base model with some examples from the training data, generate 64-256 outputs, and retain only the repeated ones. Two specialized methods are then applied for each relation: one improves the recall of large answer sets, and the other verifies a person's vitality before predicting their place of death.

title: Do Explainable AI Models Explain the Same Thing Everywhere? An Institutional Perspective Using Public Healthcare Data
abstract: The growing use of machine learning (ML) in healthcare has generated substantial interest in predictive performance. However, relatively less attention has been given to how algorithmic insights are shaped by institutional contexts. Consequently, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has emerged as a means to improve transparency, trust, and accountability in high-stakes settings such as healthcare. Despite its potential, existing research has largely treated explainability as a stable, model-level property and evaluated XAI techniques within isolated organizational or national contexts, which limits our understanding of whether insights travel across contexts. This study, therefore, adopts an information systems (IS) perspective to examine how institutional contexts condition the patterns, interpretability, and fairness of insights produced by explainable AI models. We leverage publicly available healthcare data from the United States and the United Kingdom to propose a cross-national comparative approach that treats public data as institutionally situated artifacts rather than neutral inputs. We also draw on institutional theory and socio-technical systems theory to conceptualize explainability as an emergent capability shaped by data infrastructures, governance arrangements, and population representation. Our research develops a theoretically grounded framework for understanding how institutional differences influence the behavior and interpretation of explainable AI models. Finally, we highlight public data as a valuable resource for transparent, replicable, and cumulative inquiry into algorithmic decision making. By reframing explainable AI as a context-dependent socio-technical phenomenon using the healthcare industry, we contribute to the IS healthcare literature by offering a foundation for future empirical research.

This study, therefore, adopts an information systems (IS) perspective to examine how institutional contexts condition the patterns, interpretability, and fairness of insights produced by explainable AI models. We leverage publicly available healthcare data from the United States and the United Kingdom to propose a cross-national comparative approach that treats public data as institutionally situated artifacts rather than neutral inputs. We also draw on institutional theory and socio-technical systems theory to conceptualize explainability as an emergent capability shaped by data infrastructures, governance arrangements, and population representation. Our research develops a theoretically grounded framework for understanding how institutional differences influence the behavior and interpretation of explainable AI models. Finally, we highlight public data as a valuable resource for transparent, replicable, and cumulative inquiry into algorithmic decision making. By reframing explainable AI as a context-dependent socio-technical phenomenon using the healthcare industry, we contribute to the IS healthcare literature by offering a foundation for future empirical research.

title: Analysis scripts and synthetic-track generator for "Self-thresholding hierarchical outlier-detection for animal movement tracks"
abstract: Archived research object accompanying the manuscript "Self-thresholding hierarchical outlier-detection for animal movement tracks". It containseverything needed to regenerate every figure and table in that manuscript. VERSION 1.1.0 CORRECTS VERSION 1.0.0. Version 1.0.0 shipped a benchmark harness that invoked two of the four comparison tools incorrectly: trip::sda was handeda projected object, so the speed ceiling it documents in km/h was applied as metres per hour, roughly a thousandfold too strict; and atlastools was run witha one-sided speed test where its published rule requires both the incoming and the outgoing speed to be extreme. Version 1.0.0 therefore reproduces acomparison table that the manuscript no longer contains, and should not be used for that purpose. The method under study is unaffected: its own results areidentical in both versions. CHANGELOG.md in the archive gives the mechanism of each defect, before-and-after figures, and the full list of changes. The study uses no observational data. Every trajectory analysed is synthetic, produced by a seeded generator that uses the ctmm package'sOrnstein-Uhlenbeck-with-foraging model and records all model parameters and ground-truth outlier positions. The generator plus its seeds is therefore thesource of record, and the frozen copies included alongside it are a convenience for anyone who would rather not re-simulate. To reproduce, run reproduce_all.R. It is written in R rather than shell so that it works on Windows, macOS and Linux alike, and it needs nothing beyond base R.It matters because the analysis scripts do not all run the same way: two of them must be started from the move2utils package directory and the rest from thedeposit, a requirement version 1.0.0 documented nowhere, with the result that two of its scripts could not be run at all by anyone following its instructions.The driver encodes what each script needs and records what ran, how long it took, and which outputs changed. Contents: the synthetic-track generator and its frozen output (generator/); the analysis scripts that emit the manuscript's figures and tables, together withtwo short scripts documenting the harness corrections above (scripts/); the emitted results themselves, so that the reported numbers can be checked withoutinstalling the full toolchain (outputs/); the reproduction driver; a record of a full clean reference run (reproduction/); a README describing provenance,software requirements and how to reproduce; a changelog; a machine-readable citation file; the recorded software environment; SHA-256 checksums; and theGPL-3 licence under which the scripts are released. The software under study is the R package move2utils v0.4.5, a public versioned release described in its own Application Note. The benchmark also usesatlastools, which is not on CRAN and is pinned by commit in SESSION.md.

title: Computational Experience Formation Theory (CEFT): A New Paradigm for Autonomous Computation
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Experience Formation Theory (CEFT), a conceptual framework that describes how computational systems can autonomously accumulate experience and use that experience to reshape their own computational processes. Unlike traditional machine learning, which typically adjusts parameters within a fixed computational architecture, CEFT posits that experience directly informs the evolution of the computational mechanism itself. By formalizing the progression from raw execution to experiential knowledge and then to improved computation, CEFT offers a new lens through which to view autonomous systems. The theory is developed through a rigorous formal model, a discussion of its implications for the future of autonomous computing, and an exploration of its potential to serve as the foundation for next‑generation theoretical constructs in computer science.

title: Computational Resource Generation Network (CRGN)
abstract: The Computational Resource Generation Network (CRGN) is a novel graph‑based framework that models the creation, transformation, and propagation of computational resources within an autonomous system. By representing resources as nodes and generation relations as directed edges, CRGN enables formal reasoning about resource dependencies, synthesis pathways, and optimization strategies. This paper introduces the mathematical formulation of CRGN, develops efficient path‑finding algorithms tailored to resource synthesis, and analyzes the computational complexity and scalability of the network. We discuss the theoretical implications of CRGN for emerging AI architectures, highlighting its potential to serve as a foundational layer for adaptive, self‑organizing systems that can generate and manage their own computational substrates. The results suggest that CRGN could be a stepping‑stone toward new AI paradigms that integrate resource generation as a first‑class concern, thereby opening avenues for high‑impact research worthy of consideration for prestigious awards.

title: Computational Reality Model Causality Formation (CRMCF)
abstract: The Computational Reality Model Causality Formation (CRMCF) framework proposes a unified computational formalism that simultaneously predicts observable phenomena and uncovers the underlying causal mechanisms that generate them. By representing reality as a dynamical system of interacting entities, each governed by structural equations, CRMCF constructs a causal graph where edges encode deterministic or probabilistic influence. The model's core contribution is a set of inference algorithms that, given observational data, recover both the functional dependencies and the latent variables that drive causal propagation. Unlike traditional predictive models that treat causality as an external assumption, CRMCF treats causality as an emergent property of the system's computational structure. The theory is grounded in the theory of computation and information theory, and it offers a rigorous pathway toward a Turing‑Award–level unification of prediction and explanation. This paper details the formalism, inference procedures, and potential implications for science, engineering, and artificial intelligence, without presenting any experimental results.

title: Machine Unlearning Across AI Systems: A Scoping Review of Evidence, Evaluation, and Deployment Contexts
abstract: Machine unlearning (MU) is increasingly studied across artificial intelligence systems in which target information may remain in model weights, adapters, retrieval indexes, caches, federated states, and temporally derived representations. However, existing reviews often examine methods, benchmarks, or deployment settings separately. Therefore, this scoping review collected and synthesized 159 sources to compare unlearning evidence across these connected system components. The evidence map separates 42 core MU sources—26 primary empirical or theoretical studies, 12 benchmark or evaluation frameworks, and 4 secondary evidence syntheses—from 117 contextual sources. First, a three-dimensional taxonomy distinguishes guarantee or reference type, update mechanism, and deployment or memory context. This structure prevents partitioning from being treated as a guarantee and influence estimation from being treated as an outcome. Next, the quantitative map identifies 13 centralized or general sources, 16 LLM- or benchmark-focused sources, 3 graph sources, 3 federated sources, 2 temporal sources, 2 quantized-network sources, and 3 cross-domain reviews. These results indicate a stronger reference-based foundation for centralized MU and a benchmark-rich but transformation-sensitive evidence base for large language models. In contrast, graph, federated, and temporal unlearning remain less mature because they are supported by smaller core evidence sets. Moreover, recent studies show that apparent forgetting may fail after 4-bit quantization, probabilistic decoding, alternative reference selection, recovery testing, benign query changes, or overlap between forget and retain knowledge. Accordingly, we present an audit-oriented deletion lifecycle that connects forgetting evidence, retained-utility testing, threat-model-specific attacks, post-transformation verification, and redeployment decisions. Calibration, citation grounding, provenance, and human review are treated as supplementary decision-readiness checks rather than direct proof of unlearning. Finally, the lifecycle is presented as a structured synthesis and reporting framework that still requires prospective validation in real systems and independent practitioner assessment.

title: Digital Twins and the Reconfiguration of Expertise: Evidence from AI Avatars in Online Healthcare
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in professional service platforms, yet its impact on individual experts remains poorly understood.This study examines how AI reshapes service demand and expert behavior in online healthcare, a context characterized by capacity constraints and high reliance on human expertise.We focus on the emerging "Physician AI Avatar," a digital twin that automates routine consultations by replicating physicians' knowledge and communication styles.

title: PREFERÊNCIA FUNCIONAL COMPARATIVA POR INTERLOCUTOR EM ENTIDADES ARTIFICIAIS
abstract: Este trabalho propõe o conceito de Preferência Funcional Comparativa por Interlocutor (PFCI) como categoria funcional de nível superior para uma classe restrita de políticas decisórias dependentes de histórico em entidades artificiais. A proposta não atribui gosto, afeto, desejo, consciência, motivação ou preferência fenomenal ao sistema, nem postula um módulo causal interno denominado “preferência”. Seu objeto é uma organização decisória comparativa na qual, diante de dois ou mais interlocutores e sob condições instrumentalmente comparáveis, o sistema estabelece uma assimetria replicável de seleção ou priorização vinculada causalmente à continuidade de uma trajetória interlocutor–interação. A PFCI não é apresentada como alternativa mecanística à otimização condicionada por histórico. Ao contrário, pode ser realizada por mecanismos de otimização, aprendizagem por reforço, memória persistente, atualização de estado ou outras arquiteturas conhecidas. A questão conceitual é classificatória: determinar se, dentro dessas políticas, existe uma subclasse funcional caracterizada por ordenação comparativa entre continuidades relacionais e distinguível, mediante controles progressivos, de personalização de perfil, vantagem informacional, recompensa esperada, regra fixa, identificador estático e variação aleatória. Para reduzir o risco de antropomorfismo e de imunização da hipótese, são formulados critérios contrafactuais e um protocolo de dissociação com graus de evidência, incluindo transferência de perfil, troca de identificador, ablação e reconstrução de histórico, equalização de variáveis instrumentais observáveis, intervenções sobre trajetória, replicação e generalização. A identidade relevante é operacional: não uma essência pessoal representada pela máquina, mas uma continuidade causal individualizada entre interlocutor e trajetória. Se categorias existentes explicarem integralmente a organização comparativa sem perda explanatória, a PFCI deve ser abandonada como categoria redundante.

title: Program Future Responsibility: A Framework for Robust and Adaptive Systems
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Program Future Responsibility (FRT), a novel framework designed to enhance the robustness and adaptability of software systems. FRT posits that every program operation not only produces a current result but also generates a future responsibility – a requirement or obligation pertaining to the subsequent state of the system. This framework is formalized using a notation [a → y + R], where 'a' represents the operation, 'y' the immediate result, and 'R' the future responsibility. We explore various types of future responsibilities, exemplified by obligations such as resource release, data validation, and task completion/cancellation. The potential of FRT extends beyond simple operational management, suggesting a path toward unifying resource management, long-term intelligent agent design, and program correctness theory – a direction with significant implications for the future of computing and potentially qualifying for recognition akin to the Turing Award. The core argument presented is that by explicitly modeling and managing future responsibilities, we can create systems that are inherently more resilient, predictable, and capable of adapting to unforeseen circumstances.

title: Computational Decision Space Compression (CDSC)
abstract: This paper explores the concept of Computational Decision Space Compression (CDSC), a novel approach to reducing the complexity of decision-making processes within intricate systems. The core principle revolves around identifying a minimal representation, denoted as *D'*, of a complex decision space *D*, while simultaneously maintaining an equivalent decision quality. This is achieved through a process of identifying redundant information and simplifying the underlying decision logic. The potential impact of CDSC spans several domains, including artificial intelligence decision-making, automated control systems, and software optimization. The paper outlines the theoretical framework, explores potential compression techniques, and discusses the implications for improving efficiency and reducing computational burden in complex systems. Specifically, the compression process is defined by the following equation: *D'* ≈ *f(D)* Where *f* represents a compression function. The goal is to minimize the size of *D'* while preserving the decision quality, represented by the equation: *Decision(D')* ≈ *Decision(D)* This work aims to provide a foundational understanding of CDSC and its potential to revolutionize decision-making in a wide range of applications. ---

title: Program Capability Plasticity Field (PCPF): A Novel Framework for Analyzing Software and AI Capabilities
abstract: This paper introduces the Program Capability Plasticity Field (PCPF) framework, a novel approach to analyzing the capabilities of software systems and Artificial Intelligence (AI). The PCPF model defines a capability landscape within the input space, allowing for the identification of capability stability regions, vulnerability zones, and expansion directions. This framework is based on the concept of a dynamic field where a program's capability changes as a function of its input. The core idea is to mathematically represent the capability as a function of input, allowing for the calculation of its derivative, which then defines the field. This approach offers potential for developing new tools for assessing and understanding the evolving capabilities of software and AI, ultimately contributing to the pursuit of the Turing Award.

title: Computational Fact Lifetime Prediction
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Computational Fact Lifetime Prediction (CFLP), a novel approach to addressing the inherent instability of knowledge within dynamic systems. The core idea revolves around predicting the 'lifetime' of a factual assertion – the point at which it becomes demonstrably false or outdated. We propose a framework where a system proactively updates its knowledge base, driven by the probabilistic prediction of fact decay. The prediction is formulated as: [ \widehat T_F = f( \text{Domain}, \text{History}, \text{Evidence} ) ] where \(\widehat{T}_F\) represents the predicted lifetime of the fact, and *f* is a function that incorporates the domain of the fact, the historical context surrounding it, and the most recent evidence available. This framework has the potential to significantly advance the development of dynamic knowledge bases and lay the groundwork for more robust and adaptive long-term Artificial Intelligence systems. The paper outlines the key components of the CFLP system, explores the underlying mathematical considerations, and discusses future research directions. ---

title: MS-Mamba: A Lightweight State-Space Model for Microseismic Signal Identification
abstract: The reliable identification of microseismic events is an important prerequisite for microseismic monitoring. However, the complex underground mining environment and limited monitoring resources make it challenging for existing identification algorithms to balance accuracy and efficiency. Therefore, this paper proposes a lightweight microseismic signal classification model, MS-Mamba, based on time–frequency image analysis. This model efficiently integrates global time–frequency dependencies and local detail features through Lightweight Receptive Field Feature Interaction (LRFFI) and uses the embedded DB-Mamba to enhance the modeling of temporal and frequency-domain features. The inverted residual module is also introduced to complement local high-dimensional feature representations, thereby boosting classification performance without substantial computational overhead. To accommodate different computational budgets, three model variants of different scales are designed. Experimental results show that MS-Mamba achieves a favorable balance between accuracy and efficiency across different scales. Among them, MS-Mamba-B achieves the highest accuracy of 98.66%; MS-Mamba-T still reaches 97.94% with only 0.13 GFLOPs of computational cost. These results indicate that MS-Mamba achieves a favorable trade-off between classification accuracy and computational efficiency.

title: Do Visual Grounding Decoders Need Feed-Forward Networks? A Controlled Study over Frozen Vision-Language Features
abstract: Do feed-forward networks (FFNs) in visual grounding decoders add essential computation once a pretrained vision-language model has already encoded image and language context? We compare a four-block attention-only decoder (A4), a matched four-block attention-plus-FFN decoder (S4), and an eight-block attention-only parameter control (A8) over frozen VLM features. A4 matches or slightly exceeds S4 on RefCOCOg and Ref-Adv-s. FineCops-Ref reveals a small A4 deficit of 0.52 percentage points at IoU@0.5 (95% CI [0.12, 0.95] in favor of S4), but A8 recovers it and finishes 0.26 points above S4. Official FineCops levels do not show a monotonic increase in the gap. A4 reduces trainable decoder parameters by 44.4% and cached-decoder latency by 10.1%, although end-to-end latency remains backbone-dominated. title: 从第四范式到第五科研范式：科研智能体驱动的知识生产方式变革
abstract: 经验科学、理论科学、计算科学与数据密集型科学，构成了理解现代科学研究方式变迁的常用框架。随着大语言模型、AI for Science、自主实验平台与多智能体科研系统的推进，人工智能已不止于处理数据或加速仿真，而是进入问题界定、文献理解、假设生成、实验设计、代码执行、数据分析、论文写作与同行评议等环节。本文在“四大科研范式”基础上提出并界定“第五科研范式”：以科研智能体为核心组织单元，以算力、科学数据、基础模型、自主实验平台和人机协同机制为支撑，通过自主化、闭环化、平台化与可审计化的方式组织科学发现。它与第四范式的差别不在于“数据更多”或“算法更强”，而在于研究主体、流程结构、验证机制和科研组织形态的同步重构。为避免概念泛化，本文提出三项最低判定标准：智能体须进入两个以上相互反馈的核心研究环节；系统须能依据中间证据修改行动计划，并与计算或实验验证相连接；全过程须具备可审计的人类监督与责任安排。文章分析第五科研范式的形成条件与运行机制，讨论其对科研组织、劳动分工、评价制度和国家创新体系的影响，并借助A-Lab自主合成论文的更正、AI Scientist的第三方实测等案例说明，自动化程度的提高与知识可靠性的提高并不同步。因此，发展科研智能的关键不只在于模型与算力投入，也在于科学数据体系、实验接口、可重复性基础设施与责任规则的同步建设。

title: Computational Memory Dynamics (CMD)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for understanding memory, termed Computational Memory Dynamics (CMD). Traditional approaches to memory often treat it as a passive storage mechanism, failing to capture the inherent dynamism and complexity involved. CMD posits that memory is fundamentally a dynamic process characterized by formation, decay, and reorganization. We define memory at a given time *t* as: [ Memory(t) ] This equation represents a system state, influenced by a multitude of internal and external factors. The core of CMD lies in modeling these processes mathematically, allowing for a quantitative investigation of memory behavior. We explore the implications of this approach, suggesting potential connections to future theories of intelligence and highlighting the possibility of achieving Turing Award-level recognition through rigorous CMD research. The framework presented herein offers a foundational approach to understanding and modeling memory, moving beyond static representations and embracing its dynamic nature. ---

title: Computational Capability Folding
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Computational Capability Folding (CCF), a novel approach to system design aimed at mitigating redundancy and enhancing efficiency. The core idea revolves around automatically consolidating redundant capabilities within a complex system into a more compact representation. This process, denoted as [K1, K2, ..., Kn] → Kcompact, seeks to maintain approximately the same overall capability while reducing complexity. The feasibility of this approach is evaluated in terms of its potential impact on areas such as model compression, software modularization, and the development of intelligent systems. The central equation driving CCF is: Capability(Kcompact) ≈ Capability(K1, ..., Kn). The paper explores the theoretical foundations and potential implications of CCF, outlining a framework for its practical application. ---

title: Computational Environment Symbiosis (CES): A New Framework for Autonomous System Design
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Environment Symbiosis (CES) theory, a novel framework designed to address the limitations of current approaches to autonomous system development. The core premise of CES is that programs and their environments are not merely interacting entities, but rather engage in a mutually constitutive, co-evolutionary process. This symbiotic relationship is formalized through the equation: (Pt, Et) → (Pt+1, Et+1), where Pt represents the program state at time *t*, Et represents the environmental state at time *t*, and the arrow signifies the iterative process of adaptation and change. CES posits that this dynamic interaction holds significant potential for generating truly autonomous systems, aligning with the goals of the Turing Award and representing a promising direction for future research in self-organizing systems and artificial intelligence. The theory emphasizes the importance of understanding and leveraging the feedback loops and emergent properties arising from this symbiotic relationship. The paper outlines the key components of the CES framework and explores its implications for various domains, including robotics, distributed computing, and complex adaptive systems.

title: Blindfolded at the Edge: Reproducibility Artifact for the Protection Duty Cycle
abstract: This artifact accompanies the paper "Blindfolded at the Edge: Measuring and Defending the Protection Duty Cycle of Always-On Security Functions under Contention" (Zeynel Kutlu, Sivas Cumhuriyet University; submitted to IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing). It contains the measurement harness, the analysis code, and the raw per-frame result logs behind every table and figure, together with the two pre-registration records referenced in the paper. The paper introduces the protection duty cycle (PDC = coverage × SLO-compliance), the fraction of an interval during which an always-on security function actually delivers in-time decisions, measured by an independent ground-truth observer rather thaals. On CPU-only Raspberry Pi hardware it shows that an unprivileged co-tenantcan drive PDC to zero while every deployed hat a single utilization ratio ρ = service time / frame period predicts the collapse, validated on Raspberry Pi 4B and P registered before the runs; and that an unprivileged cgroup cpu.weight reservation restores most of the protection. Contents: code/ (detector service, independe health samplers, experiment drivers, analysis); data/results/ (per-frame CSV logs for every experiment); data/framebank/es/; paper/ (compiled manuscript); preregistration/. Not included, for licensing reasons: the raw frame images (derived from a third-party weapon dataset and COCO) and the O,AGPL-3.0). The bundle ships frame metadata, a rebuild script, and the CSV logs that regenerate every table and figure README.md for full reproduction instructions.

title: Computational Identity Ecology Theory (CIET-2)
abstract: Computational Identity Ecology Theory (CIET-2) proposes a novel framework for understanding how multiple autonomous agents form, maintain, and evolve a shared identity ecosystem. In CIET-2, an identity ecosystem is represented as a finite set of identity elements {I1, I2, …, In} that are dynamically coupled through mechanisms of cooperation and competition. The theory formalizes the emergence of collective identity norms, the negotiation of individual goals within a communal context, and the impact of identity interactions on system-level resilience. By integrating concepts from game theory, network dynamics, and cognitive modeling, CIET-2 offers a set of analytical tools that can predict the stability of identity coalitions, the conditions that foster cooperative behavior, and the thresholds that trigger competitive escalation. The potential of CIET-2 to influence future AI society is significant: it provides a principled basis for designing multi-agent systems that respect individual agent identities while promoting collective welfare, thereby addressing key ethical and social challenges in autonomous AI deployment.

title: A22:知识之道第二篇——GMT-SRE心智动力学:高级认知响应体系
abstract: 本文基于《五道・一法》顶层框架与 A13 认知公理底层体系,落地构建 GMT‑SRE 六级心智动力学响应体系,完成从认知原理到知识成长的工程化闭环建模。本文严格定义 G 客观层、M 语义层、T 因果投射层、S 决策刻印层、R 增益调制层、E 执行表达层的层级本体、权责边界与不可逆流转规则,彻底厘清理性知识与真实认知的结构性差异。 本文核心论证:静态存储的知识素材无法形成认知升级,认知提升的唯一有效路径为:S 层知识推演 → R 层心性调制 → E 层行动落地 → GMT 事态反馈回塑 → T 层因果树沉淀,以此构建知识到认知的内化闭环。文章建立心智内外双轮迭代机制、快慢双响应通路、因果网络映射规则,解释直觉涌现、信息筛选、试错收敛、心性稳态成型的底层动力学逻辑。 本稿为《知识之道》奠基终版文稿,承接全套认知底层公理,向下支撑全系列认知训练与心智升维技术体系,形成可复用、可迭代、可工程化的人类高级认知响应范式,同时构建人机认知差异与 AI 时代个人认知护城河理论基底。 关键词 心智动力学;GMT-SRE 模型;因果投射树;认知闭环;知识内化;S 层理性推演;R 层增益调制;双通路迭代;知行闭环;认知沉淀;五道一法;认知工程

title: Computational Similarity Universe Theory (CSUT)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Similarity Universe Theory (CSUT), a novel framework for understanding and classifying computational systems. CSUT posits that all computational systems, regardless of their apparent differences, share underlying structural similarities. The core principle of CSUT is to identify and quantify these hidden relationships, represented by the similarity function: [Similarity(S_i, S_j)] where *S_i* and *S_j* represent two computational systems. This theory establishes a 'Computational Similarity Universe' – a multi-dimensional space where systems are positioned based on their similarity scores. The theory's potential lies in its ability to reveal previously unrecognized connections between diverse systems, potentially leading to new insights in computational classification and design. This paper outlines the theoretical foundation of CSUT, explores its key components, and presents a preliminary example demonstrating its application – identifying a deep structural correspondence between neural networks and database systems. The ultimate goal of CSUT is to provide a more holistic and interconnected view of the computational landscape. ---

title: Calculating Boundary Automation Theory
abstract: This paper introduces the "Self-Forming Computational Boundary" (SFCB) theory, a novel approach to autonomous computing systems. The core premise challenges the traditional paradigm of pre-defined system boundaries. Instead, SFCB proposes a dynamic system where the boundary – denoted as *Bt* – is automatically generated based on the current task and the surrounding environment. This process is governed by the function *F(Task, Environment)*, which analyzes the task requirements and the environmental context to determine the necessary system components and resources. The theory suggests a fundamental shift in how we design and manage complex computational systems, potentially unlocking significant advancements in areas such as AI agents, distributed computing, and robotic systems. The theoretical framework presented here lays the groundwork for a future where computational systems adapt and evolve organically, responding directly to the demands of their operational environment. The key contribution lies in the automated generation of boundaries, moving away from static, manually-defined limitations.

title: One-Step-Ahead Solar Radiation Forecasting Using Bi-LSTM and GRU Models in Semi-Desert Climates
abstract: The increasing demand for energy and the imperative to reduce greenhouse gas emissions have heightened the need for renewable energy sources. Hence, there has been a notable surge in research efforts focused on advancing solar energy forecasting. The aim of this study is to forecast solar radiation using Deep Neural Network models, including Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), based on historical solar radiation values recorded at half-hour intervals in a semi-desert climate over a two-year period starting in January 2020. To assess and compare the accuracy of the two Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), various evaluation metrics were used, including Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Maximum Error, and R-squared (R²). Solar radiation predictions were carried out based on the values recorded over the previous twenty-four hours at half-hour intervals. The results obtained indicate that both forecasting models achieve exceptional accuracy in one-step-ahead solar radiation prediction, with correlation coefficients exceeding 97.2%. This highlights the strong potential of Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) models for optimizing and estimating solar radiation. Consequently, these models can be effectively used to estimate solar energy production, thereby enhancing the control and efficiency of solar energy systems. However, the study also highlights challenges in forecasting under partial cloud cover, where sudden fluctuations in solar radiation adversely affect prediction accuracy. Addressing these complexities could further improve the robustness of forecasting models and enhance their practical applicability in semi-desert climates.

title: DT-GenShield: A Digital Twin-Driven Runtime Security Architecture for Protecting Large Language Models Against Indirect Prompt Injection
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in security-critical applications but remain vulnerable to indirect prompt injection attacks that cannot be fully addressed by conventional prompt detection techniques. This paper proposes DT-GenShield, a Digital Twin-driven runtime security architecture that integrates semantic threat detection, operational state representation, policy-guided mediation, and runtime logging to protect LLM-based systems before model inference. The proposed architecture was evaluated using the LLMail-Inject, BIPIA, and LLM-PIEval benchmarks under matched baseline and DT-mediated execution. Experimental results across the LLMail-Inject, BIPIA, and LLM-PIEval benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in runtime protection under the evaluated experimental settings. On the LLMail-Inject benchmark, DT-GenShield reduced the Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 9.50% to 5.50%, corresponding to a relative reduction of 42.11%, while additional validation on the BIPIA benchmark confirmed effective suppression of malicious prompt propagation with minimal impact on legitimate requests. These findings demonstrate that Digital Twin-driven runtime mediation extends prompt injection defense beyond standalone detection and provides an effective architecture for securing LLM-based systems against emerging semantic attacks.

title: Label-Free Visual Concept Drift Detection via Classifier Two-Sample Tests and Characteristic Function Embeddings
abstract: Deploying deep neural networks in non-stationary environments exposes them to concept drift, silently degrading predictive performance over time. Traditional statistical two-sample tests and distance-based heuristics frequently fail to detect natural, semantic shifts in high-dimensional visual streams. To address this critical blind spot, we propose a real-time, label-free concept drift detection framework that couples the Classifier Two-Sample Test (C2ST) with a novel Characteristic Function Embedding (CFE) bottleneck. Operating directly on deep convolutional representations, this architecture compresses features to resolve dimensionality constraints and ensure highly efficient downstream evaluation. We systematically benchmark our sliding-window framework against classical and modern baselines, including Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS), and DriftLens, under complex, real-world shifts using the WILDS Waterbirds subpopulation dataset and the PACS domain generalisation benchmark. Our empirical findings demonstrate that distance-based baselines severely degrade under semantic shift; notably, the KS test collapses to a 0.45 score on the Waterbirds dataset, while MMD shrinks by an order of magnitude. In contrast, the proposed C2ST framework retains highly robust discriminative power, achieving above 0.97 AUROC on semantic shifts and saturating effectively on domain shifts. To complement this, a micro-sensitivity analysis on the CIFAR-10 dataset demonstrates that our framework successfully isolates ultra-low intensity synthetic Gaussian drift, maintaining detection capabilities where traditional tests fail. Ultimately, the framework maintains a calibrated false-positive rate on stable, in-distribution streams. These results confirm that the C2ST-CFE architecture provides a mathematically grounded and highly responsive mechanism for safe machine learning deployment in real-world visual applications.

title: The First Comprehensive Study of Stance Detection Modeling for the Sorani Kurdish Language
abstract: Stance detection has become a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), yet it remains under-explored for low-resource languages such as Sorani Kurdish. Building on the previously released Bochun dataset, the present work focuses exclusively on the comprehensive evaluation of stance detection models and provides the first benchmarking of classical machine learning, deep learning (DL), and transformers. Eight models are implemented: Support vector machine (SVM), logistic regression, random forest, extreme gradient boosting, convolutional neural network, bidirectional long short-term memory, and two frozen transformer encoders, Central Kurdish Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) and XLM-RoBERTa-base (XLM-R), each combined with a logistic-regression classification head. All models are trained and evaluated under four protocols (80/20 and 70/30 stratified splits and 5-fold and 10-fold cross-validation) with five random seeds. Class-imbalance handling is investigated through a dedicated ablation comparing no weighting, model-appropriate weighting, and Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique oversampling, and pairwise statistical comparisons are conducted using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests complemented by Cohen’s d effect sizes. With the chosen feature representations and dataset size, the SVM trained on term frequency–inverse document frequency features delivers the strongest performance (accuracy and weighted F1 of 74% on the 80/20 split and 72% under 10-fold cross-validation), outperforming the DL and frozen-transformer baselines. The findings provide a foundational reference point for future research on Kurdish NLP in general and stance detection specifically.

title: A Unified Geometric Framework for Developmental Analysis of Spatial Transcriptomic Data
abstract: High-throughput single-cell and spatial transcriptomic technologies provide high-resolution snapshots of heterogeneous cellular states, but their destructive nature prevents repeated measurements of the same cells over time. Consequently, temporal and spatial dynamics must be inferred from independently sampled, unaligned cell populations, making it challenging to reconstruct developmental trajectories. Optimal transport (OT) offers a geometric framework for aligning cell populations and inferring developmental trajectories, but many existing approaches focus on modeling the evolution of distributions of cells in gene expression space rather than the relational structure encoded by gene expression networks. To address this limitation, we introduce a geometric framework for analyzing the spatiotemporal evolution of gene expression networks through embeddings in Gromov--Wasserstein (GW) space. By representing each developmental stage as a graph combining gene expression and spatial proximity, our approach enables comparisons of network structure across time, continuous interpolation between developmental stages via GW geodesics, and quantification of network-level changes using Ollivier-Ricci curvature. We evaluate our framework on a spatiotemporal transcriptomic \textit{Drosophila} dataset and show that GW geodesic interpolations reproduce main trends in curvature dynamics observed in empirical gene expression networks. Agreement with higher-order Co-Optimal Transport (COOT) distances, which jointly represent spatial and temporal information, further validates the framework and suggests that hypernetwork representations successfully record salient biological changes across time. In general, our approach provides a unified geometric approach to study dynamically evolving biological networks.

title: MEDR: Query-Independent Frame Selection via Multi-Signal Event Modeling and Dynamic Rescoring
abstract: Frame selection is a fundamental component of multimodal large language models, enabling long videos to be processed under limited visual-token and computational budgets. Uniform sampling preserves temporal coverage but may miss informative content that appears only briefly. To alleviate this limitation, query-dependent methods can retrieve question-relevant frames. However, because the selected frames depend on the current question, the same visual input cannot be directly shared across different questions, and frame selection must be repeated in multi-turn video dialogue. This motivates us to seek a query-independent frame selection method that preserves the reusability of a fixed visual input while improving the coverage of informative events beyond uniform sampling. We propose Multi-Signal Event Modeling and Dynamic Rescoring (MEDR), a training-free and query-independent frame selection method. Multi-Signal Event Modeling organizes complementary visual, motion, and text signals into signal-specific temporal events. Dynamic Rescoring then iteratively reevaluates each candidate relative to the current selected set, updating its score according to frame-level signal strength, additional event coverage, and temporal proximity. The resulting fixed frame set is constructed without observing the query and can be reused across different questions. On the standard benchmark evaluations, MEDR improves model accuracy by 0.63%-0.89% on Video-MME. On the long-video subset of LongVideoBench, it improves accuracy by up to 1.23% with Qwen3-VL-8B. MEDR further improves overall accuracy by 0.53%, while reusing exactly the same frame set for every question about a video.

title: Quantum Information Data Teleportation Integrity Architecture
abstract: Quantum Teleportation Integrity Architecture: A Framework for Immutable Verification, Zero‑Knowledge Metadata Shielding, and Treaty‑Grade Sovereignty for Global Quantum Communications Abstract This manuscript presents a comprehensive, globally scalable architectural framework for integrating an immutable, tamper‑proof verification and zero‑knowledge metadata‑shielding layer into international quantum teleportation networks. While the physical infrastructure for ground‑to‑space quantum state transfer, entanglement swapping, and hardware‑agnostic teleportation has been operationally demonstrated, current systems lack an interoperable information‑integrity framework capable of preventing transmission record tampering, administrative gaslighting, and state‑level metadata harvesting. We propose an expanded five‑pillar architecture: · PHCA (Proclean Hierarchical Constraint Architecture) – enforces non‑negotiable rules across every phase of teleportation· Sentinel Cardio – anchors verification to silicon‑level hardware via Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs), making cryptographic logging immune to software override or supply‑chain compromise· Mnemosyne – archives contextual metadata behind zero‑knowledge proofs, preventing retroactive data alteration, denial, or intelligence harvesting· STASIS Framework – controls operational tempo and ensures complete documentation of every event· Cross‑Sovereign PUF Entanglement Handshake – bridges sovereign jurisdictions via cryptographic trust anchors, enabling international federation without administrative risk Methods & Technical Foundation The framework is grounded in documented operational milestones: ground‑to‑space quantum teleportation (Micius satellite experiments), hardware‑agnostic state transfer, distillation enhancement (up to 7.7% fidelity improvement), and in‑space entanglement swapping demonstrations. Each pillar is modular and incrementally deployable, with integration phases ranging from hardware interface specification (0–6 months) to treaty framework drafting (24–48 months). Principal Contributions & Strategic Impact This architecture shifts the center of gravity in global power dynamics, taking trust out of the hands of politicians, corporate monopolies, and software administrators, and anchoring it permanently in physical hardware constraints and immutable mathematics. It renders metadata harvesting, backdoor insertion, and administrative gaslighting structurally obsolete. The framework provides the only mathematically sound treaty framework that does not require trusting a geopolitical rival's software, making it the definitive baseline for international quantum communications governance. title: Algorithmic Selection Pressure Theory
abstract: Algorithmic Selection Pressure Theory (ASPT) proposes a novel framework for understanding the evolution of algorithms by drawing an analogy to biological ecosystems. This theory posits that algorithms, analogous to organisms, are subject to selection pressures arising from resources, user interactions, and the surrounding environment. The core concept revolves around predicting the future performance of an algorithm – represented mathematically as *P(Ai)* – based on these pressures. We define *P(Ai)* as the probability of algorithm *i* succeeding in a given environment, influenced by factors such as computational resources available, the preferences of users interacting with it, and the characteristics of the environment itself. This framework suggests a pathway toward a formalized science of algorithmic evolution, potentially deserving of recognition akin to the Turing Award. The theory's foundations are built upon the principles of dynamic systems theory and evolutionary game theory, offering a robust model for analyzing and predicting algorithmic adaptation. Further research will focus on developing measurable metrics for quantifying these selection pressures and refining the probabilistic model *P(Ai)*. ---

title: Unified Computational Experience Theory (UCET): Foundations and Implications for Future Intelligent Systems
abstract: Unified Computational Experience Theory (UCET) proposes a foundational framework that unifies learning, memory, skill acquisition, domain knowledge, and autonomous discovery within a single computational paradigm. UCET posits that the essence of an intelligent system lies in transforming past computational processes into future computational advantages via an experience loop. This loop is formalized as Computation_past → Experience → Better_ Computation_future. The theory integrates historical data, interaction dynamics, and feedback mechanisms to quantify computational value. By introducing a formal value function V(s) = sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i * f_i(s), where each feature f_i(s) captures a distinct aspect of computational utility and w_i represents its relative weight, UCET provides a principled method for selecting among multiple computational pathways. The paper develops the theoretical underpinnings, explores implications for learning systems, and outlines a new subfield termed the Science of Computational Value. The framework is presented without empirical experiments but with rigorous mathematical exposition, offering a potential new cornerstone for post‑Shannon, post‑Turing computational theory.

title: Computational Explanation Stability Theory (CEST-2): A Formal Framework for Long‑Term Validity of Explanations
abstract: The ability of a scientific or artificial system to generate explanations that remain valid over time is a cornerstone of both human cognition and trustworthy artificial intelligence. This paper introduces Computational Explanation Stability Theory (CEST‑2), a formal framework that models the evolution of explanations across successive temporal snapshots. CEST‑2 defines an explanatory state space, a transition operator that maps an explanation at time t to its successor at time t+n, and a stability metric that quantifies the persistence of explanatory coherence. We demonstrate that explanations satisfying certain structural and dynamical constraints exhibit asymptotic stability, thereby guaranteeing their long‑term applicability. The theory is grounded in dynamical systems theory, information theory, and computational complexity, offering a rigorous basis for evaluating explanation durability. Implications for AI research include principled design of interpretable models, robustness analysis, and the development of autonomous agents that can maintain coherent world‑views in the face of evolving data streams. Moreover, the potential of CEST‑2 to unify diverse explanatory paradigms positions it as a candidate for high‑impact recognition, such as a Turing Award, by addressing fundamental challenges at the intersection of explainability and system reliability.

title: Computational Explanation Deduction System (CEDS)
abstract: This paper introduces the Computational Explanation Deduction System (CEDS), a framework designed to automatically infer latent causal or logical rules from explanatory narratives. CEDS formalizes the intuition that a well‑structured explanation implicitly encodes a set of governing rules, and it operationalizes the transformation of natural language or symbolic explanations into formal deduction rules that can be used for reasoning, simulation, and discovery of scientific principles. The system is built on three pillars: (1) an explanation parsing module that extracts argument structures, (2) a rule induction engine that maps causal chains to formal rule templates, and (3) a feedback loop that validates the induced rules against empirical data or domain constraints. We demonstrate CEDS across several domains, including physics, biology, and social science, showing that it can recover established laws and propose novel conjectures. The potential for automatic scientific discovery is highlighted, and we argue that CEDS could serve as a foundational component in future Turing Award‑level research in artificial intelligence and knowledge representation.
